speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY ACT AND RELATED STATUTES AND RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time after the appointment of Mr. T. D. MacDonald, K.C., as the present commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act, he requested that a committee be convened for the purpose of studying the act and recommending whether it could be made a more effective instrument. I have agreed with his request, and a committee has been set up accordingly comprising the following members: Hon. Mr. Justice J. H. MacQuarrie, Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, Halifax; Dr. W. A. Mackintosh, vice-principal of Queen's university, Kingston; Professor Maurice Lamontagne, assistant director of the department of economics, Laval university, Quebec; and Mr. George F. Curtis, dean of the university of British Columbia law school, Vancouver.
The terms of reference are to study, in the light of present day conditions, the purposes and methods of the Combines Investigation Act and related Canadian statutes, the legislation and procedures of other countries, in
so far as the latter appear likely to afford assistance, and to recommend what amendments, if any, should be made to our Canadian legislation in order to make it a more effective instrument for the encouraging and safeguarding of our free economy.
To avoid any possible misunderstanding, I desire to emphasize that no suggestions of amendments are being made to the committee for its consideration. It is the practice, however, to take stock of such acts from time to time to see whether any modifications should be considered in the light of administrative experience, changed conditions or otherwise. It is for such a purpose that this study has been arranged.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE General-Dominion coal board -
449. Administration and investigations of the dominion coal board, $101,040.

This board is relatively new, and I believe is a very important organization. We have done a great deal in the way of probing and searching the coal industry of Canada in the last few years. We had a royal commission that sat for about eighteen months and brought in a long report containing many recommendations with respect to the rehabilitation and modernization of the coal industry, particularly stressing the possibilities of marketing our coal. This board arose from that very expensive report; that was one of the recommendations of the royal commission. Of course it had been advocated in this house for many years previously, but the royal commission definitely pointed out the desirability of setting up a national coal board for the purpose of coordinating the industry across the country.
The legislation creating that board set out definite duties and responsibilities it was to undertake. It has a capable chairman, but I do not like the set-up with respect to representation from the industry and from those who produce the coal. I believe it is top-heavy with coal operators, and has very little representation from the men who dig the coal; in fact, it is four to one. Nevertheless the board has certain duties and responsibilities. It is doing some work, I admit, in the regulation of subventions, seeing that the money granted by parliament for purposes of expansion is spent properly, and so on. Meetings have been held in the coal-operating sections of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at least, and I believe at the present time the board is engaged in a survey of the coal industry in the United States.
That is all to the good; but one definite responsibility placed upon that board has not been even touched. I refer to the responsibility of devising ways and means of

marketing Canadian coal, to put the industry in a better position than it has been for years past. That is the matter I am going to bring to the attention of the minister.
We import a huge amount of coal from the United States, while if our industry were operating at capacity we could produce perhaps one-third of our own requirements. We have made some progress by way of granting money as loans to the eastern operators for the purpose of modernizing the old collieries still in operation; and the whole trend has been to reduce costs. I am not going to argue that point, but I am convinced that it is not possible to reduce costs in the old collieries of Nova Scotia to any appreciable extent because of the long haul and the high pumping and power costs, which in my opinion are the main disabilities.
As I see it the problem has always been one of marketing. Back in the thirties and up until the outbreak of the war the industry in Nova Scotia was working two or three days per week, practically on a relief basis. When war commenced the demand for coal permitted full-time operations, but soon after the war the industry slumped back to parttime operations. Regardless of whether we increase production, the main problem so far as Nova Scotia is concerned is the problem of marketing. There are no assured markets. There is a hit or miss arrangement which prevents the operators, the customers, or the employees in the industry from making any definite long-range plan.
Before his estimates are concluded I want the minister to tell us what the dominion coal board is doing in the matter of providing long-range markets on a permanent basis for Canadian coal. On many occasions I ha:,m said in this house that that can be done only by a zoning of markets in Canada in which Canadian coal could reasonably compete with United States coal. From time to time the opinion has been expressed that there is no economic market in Canada for Canadian coal; that it is a straight matter of assisting coal operations by way of subventions or subsidies. So far as I am concerned that illusion was shattered, and I think it should be so far as the minister is concerned, in the committee on railways and shipping before which Mr. Donald Gordon appeared. The Canadian National Railways are large consumers of coal, and Mr. Gordon was questioned about the difficulty experienced by the railway because of the stoppage of work in the United States. The railways' stockpile of coal in eastern Canada was lowered to the extent that a curtailment of traffic was necessary. Mr. Gordon assured us that so far as the Canadian
Supply-Trade and Commerce National was concerned there was an economic area for maritime coal which extended from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Coteau, about thirty miles west of Montreal. That area was never planned, for the simple reason that sixty or seventy per cent of the coal stockpiled by the railways in eastern Canada is coal from the United States. No arrangement was ever made to stockpile Canadian coal in that area, where it was available and where it was economical. There was a definite lack of planning for that Canadian market, and I want to find out if there is any planning being carried out at the present time.
Mr. Gordon pointed out to us that this year the Nova Scotia and New Brunswick coal operators could not supply the requirements of the Canadian National Railways in that area. Of course this year is an abnormal year owing to the depletion of the stockpiles and the necessity for rebuilding them. I might say that my discussions with Mr. Gordon represented the first time in my experience that officials in this country have made a practical and realistic approach to this problem. I am convinced there is an area there that can be allocated to eastern Canada on a permanent long-range basis. This area would absorb the main production of the maritimes and perhaps permit an expansion in that particular section.
The Alberta and British Columbia end does not look so good. The Canadian National is displacing the steam locomotive with the diesel and is thereby cutting into the coal market. Oil is backing the coal operators out of the picture in that area. In my own province the coal industry is the basic industry, and everything else is built around it. The steam locomotive has not been displaced by the diesel in that section, and that displacement will not take place for some considerable time. Despite the progress made in the building of that type of locomotive, the roadbed from Montreal to Halifax will not accommodate a diesel at the speed it travels. It means practically rebuilding the roadbed from Montreal east, so that the market for coal is likely to be there for some time, and advantage should be taken of it.
In order that stockpiling would be possible, the area from Montreal east should be allocated to the maritime coal industry. Although I am stressing this I do not want to make a long speech, because during the last ten years the minister and I have discussed this so often that we know each other's opinions. Mr. Gordon definitely gave me a new hope, because I feel that if such a zone is established and arrangements are made accordingly with the Canadian National

Supply-Trade and Commerce Railways, it would be a long step forward for the maritime coal operators. I want to emphasize again that it is not a matter of increasing production or lowering costs; it is a matter of permanent markets which would enable the industry and the people dependent upon the industry to plan their future with assurance. I should like the minister's comments on that particular aspect of the problem.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the duty of the coal board is to find markets for Canadian coal. I suggest to my hon. friend that the board has been doing just that. Since 1942 the coal industry in Nova Scotia has had much wider markets available than it has been able to supply. There have been small interruptions, perhaps, because of situations that can be smoothed out and will be smoothed out, such as a member of the industry not doing the marketing at the right time. I do not know of a day lost in the coal fields that has been due to any basic lack of markets for maritime coal. At the moment the difficulty is that during this year the mines will hardly be able to produce all the coal that can be used in the maritime provinces.
The policy that is being administered by the coal board is a policy of flexible subventions, watched very carefully from day to day, and directed toward all the markets that can be found for all the coal that is mined. I believe that it is a policy that is meeting the needs of the maritime coal industry, and will continue to do so. My hon. friend is aware that the government is endeavouring to step up the production of coal in the maritime provinces. To do so the government is lending the greater part of $10 million to the industry. I suggest the government would hardly be willing to take that step without being confident it can find markets for that coal.
The hon. member suggests that a zone be kept exclusively for maritime coal. The difficulty is that if a zone is marked out and reserved entirely for maritime coal, we must be certain that the maritimes can provide all the coal needed in that zone. To mark out a zone as far west as Coteau Junction at the moment would be foolish, because we know the maritimes cannot supply much more than fifty per cent of the coal required in that area this year. Then, there is the matter of keeping alive the markets that have been developed in the past. Maritime coal has been used at Arvida and as far west as Kapuskasing. I believe the industry wishes to keep maritime coal in those markets, so that if lack of other markets

should develop, those markets could be quickly reclaimed. Those are factors, perhaps not important factors, but I mention them to suggest that a rigid zoning of an area for marketing Canadian coal is not in my opinion as advantageous to the industry as a flexible market administered by a coal board that is watching the situation from day to day and enlarging the markets as the day to day situation may require.
My hon. friend mentioned the western coal situation. That situation is much more difficult today than is the maritime situation, for the reason that oil is being produced in an area alongside that which is producing coal, and there is a tendency for oil to displace coal in the markets nearest to the mines. These are the markets that are easiest for the coal industry to compete in. That situation is being watched carefully. The coal board is making an effort to find new and more distant markets to replace nearer markets that are being lost to the competitive product. Every step has been taken that I can think of to protect markets for the western industry. Nevertheless it is obvious-and I am sure it is obvious to the operators of the mines in the western area-that the production of western coal is likely to be on a reduced scale, as oil continues to make inroads into markets that were formerly held by the western coal operators.

May I give the minister a case in point? He says he is not aware of any curtailment of operations in any section of the maritimes because of lack of markets. On Friday of last week I received a letter from the board member of the united mine workers at Inverness. That is an operation that has been carried on by the provincial government for the last twenty years. Their main market in the past has been the C.N.R. This board member wrote to me-and I sent the letter on to the coal board-to the effect that they were practically closed down, that there was drastic curtailment of operations, and that the reason was lack of demand from the Canadian National Railways. He asked me to check here to see if there was not a possibility of arranging for the marketing of that particular coal with the C.N.R. I sent that letter along to the coal board. But that is one spot that I can mention.
I might say to the minister that it is the small operator who gets caught. The big fellow can look after himself, negotiate his contracts and fix the price with the railroads; and in many cases it is a price with which the small operator cannot compete. So far as the small operator is concerned there is reason there for the board to take hold and to see if it cannot work out some reasonable

arrangements for the small operators. I am not excusing the provincial government; they are the operators. The operation is carried on to maintain a fairly large community, and for no other reason. On economic grounds I do not think it could justify itself, but on humanitarian grounds it has been operated for years. I think the provincial government should have sufficient influence with the C.N.R. to arrange a market for the amount of coal that is produced in that particular community.

The coal board is aware of the Inverness situation, as I am myself. The difficulty there is the quality of the coal produced. The railroad would be delighted to take the coal if it were up to railroad specifications, but I think my hon. friend will agree that the coal board cannot insist that a customer take a quality of coal that is not up to the standard required by the service he operates.
My hon. friend suggests that it is the small mine operator who is being squeezed. I suggest to him that the province of Nova Scotia is no small operator-
They operate on a small scale.

-and that it is well able to market coal if the coal is of a quality that is salable. But we are aware of the Inverness situation. It is an unhappy one. The operation lost $200,000 last year, and I do not know what the outcome is to be. Fortunately the provincial government is dealing with the problem.

I did not want to interrupt
the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the minister as they were discussing this matter. I largely agree with what both have said. In his reply to the hon. member I am pleased that the minister included some remarks with respect to western coal. I am glad he recognizes the fact that the western coal mine operators are fearful that the use of oil may almost put them out of business. During the last few months there has been some considerable curtailment in the production of bituminous coal in western Canada, partly owing to the fact that the railroads are beginning to convert their locomotives to diesels. I know that we have to trust the minister in these matters. It is pleasant to hear him say that the coal board is watching the situation closely; but I do not know how much hope that sort of phraseology is going to give to the coal mining industry of western Canada. Concealed within that phraseology may be a good deal of mystery as to the future of the coal mining industry in that part of the country.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
During this session the minister indicated that he was anxious to have the pipe lines bills passed. I am not going to say anything about that matter; but in his anxiety to have the pipe lines bills passed he must have also recognized the fact that even the pipe lines and the export of oil would have some repercussions in the coal mining industry. We know that we cannot stand in the way of progress. As time goes on and as civilization passes from one era to another there are discoveries and developments, and one thing supersedes another. At the same time I think it is the responsibility of government to guard industry as much as possible, even in the light of the development of new things which might displace the industries of the past. But I believe there could be another solution to this problem. Canada is not as broadly industrialized today as it might be. Nearly all the industries in Canada are fairly well concentrated in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. If the government, as the minister says, is watching the situation carefully, I think some consideration should be given to the greater industrialization of western Canada. The more industry we can have in western Canada, the greater will be the opportunity for the coal mining industry to survive; therein lies the opportunity, in my opinion, for additional markets for western coal. But to industrialize western Canada I know is a tremendous job. The provinces of the west are doing all they can to encourage industrialization. The government should give more tangible aid in the industrialization of western Canada.
I rose to ask a particular question, and I trust the minister may be able to answer it. When the government requires coal for its own purposes, such as the purpose of defence, at training stations and other government-operated enterprises, tenders are called for. As I understand it, the Canadian Commercial Corporation is the institution used for the purpose of preparing those tenders. I hold in my hand an "Invitation to Tender"-that is the title of the document. These go out to the various coal mining interests when it is coal that the government requires.
My attention has been called to the fact that the description given in the invitation to tender is such that certain coal mines that could supply an equivalent grade of coal, or a coal that would compare most favourably with that description, might be ruled out because the mines could not supply coal of the actual name and grade given in the description. The suggestion that has come to me, and perhaps it has come to the coal board also, is that in the description the phrase "or the equivalent grade" should be

Supply-Trade and Commerce added, thus enabling other coal mines to put in their bids and have their coal of an equivalent grade stand a better chance of acceptance. I am bringing this to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will pass it on to the coal board in some favourable light.
The document that I hold in my hand calls for quite a number of orders. Here is one for 800 tons, and the description is:
Coal-bituminous slack; 40 per cent Comox and 60 per cent Drumheller or McLeod. Suitable for use in low pressure steam boilers (stoker fired).
If the phrase "or equivalent" were added, it would not rule out some of the companies from the bids. Here is another one: 75 tons-a small order; nevertheless we have small mines too that might benefit from being able to secure an order of that kind. Here is another for 300 tons, and another for 25 tons, and so forth. I do not suppose this is the only invitation to tender that there is. There may be a great deal more coal required than what is called for in this invitation. I wonder whether the minister would give favourable consideration to this suggestion, so that other coal mines would not necessarily be obviously ruled out from bidding.

It is my understanding that public tenders specify the B.T.U. value of coal, the moisture content and the ash content; that samples of coal are tested before the purchase is made, and the best value for the money is accepted. However, I shall be glad to call the attention of the Canadian Commercial Corporation to the remarks of my hon. friend and changes can be made that will not prejudice the right of the government to obtain the best value in the coal offered. If the tenders are restrictive in any way, I will see that the situation is remedied.

I quite agree that the government should get the very best value for their money, because they are spending taxpayers' money. I want to thank the minister for passing the suggestion on to the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

As the minister knows, we have a very small coal area in New Brunswick. It may not be important in the general picture, but it is very important to our province. We have had difficulties right through the piece so far as operating and selling coal are concerned, although as the minister knows we supply only about fifty per cent of the coal that is used in our own province.
Like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I appreciate what the dominion coal board has done. We have a New Brunswick


representative on that board, which I think is giving very good satisfaction so far as our producers are concerned.
I might say that the only benefit that the coal operators in our province received from the Carroll commission report was the adoption of the recommendation that a dominion coal board be set up. The Carroll report mentioned many of the difficulties which we have in New Brunswick in the matter of the operation of coal mines, but I do not think it suggested any solution.
There is the general impression that subventions help the coal industry in New Brunswick to quite an extent. That was true some years ago, during the war, when we sold quite a lot of coal outside the province. But today, as the minister probably knows, the subvention that we receive for the carrying of coal in New Brunswick is very small. In 1948 and 1949 only 864 tons of coal were sold outside the province for which we received subventions. The amount we received was $693. It is practically nothing. Therefore in the matter of subventions New Brunswick is not receiving any assistance to amount to anything. In the same year Nova Scotia sold 144,332 tons of coal and received $1,008,934. My point is this, Mr. Chairman. New Brunswick coal would receive subvention assistance if it were sold outside the province, yet we have to compete with coal coming from Nova Scotia which receives subvention in New Brunswick, and the result is that Nova Scotia coal in some instances is carried to certain points of our province cheaper than our own coal can be carried. I do not know whether representations have been made to the minister, but it has occurred to me that if he wishes to assist the operators in the coal industry of New Brunswick we might be granted subventions in that province so as to place us on an equal footing in that respect with the coal from Nova Scotia. We have no objection to Nova Scotia coal coming into New Brunswick, but we would like to be in the same position as they are so far as transportation costs are concerned.
I suggest the government should exercise great care in connection with the supply of coal for public buildings in the different provinces. A short time ago tenders were called to supply coal for public buildings in New Brunswick, and the specification was for Nova Scotia coal. New Brunswick coal was not asked for. I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this fact and in very short time he remedied it. But in matters of this kind I suggest it should not be necessary to call the attention of the department to this situation. When tenders are

called for in New Brunswick, then New Brunswick coal should be specified.
Has consideration ever been given to assisting the transportation of New Brunswick coal in New Brunswick? What amount was paid Nova Scotia coal operators by way of subventions for coal carried into New Brunswick?

As the hon. member has said, there is no difficulty in finding a market for coal produced in New Brunswick. As a matter of fact New Brunswick is an exporter of coal, about 30,000 tons of the coal of that province having been marketed in the United States last year.
That was to a pulp mill in Maine.

Yes. We provided capital assistance to one operator in a substantial sum so that he could enlarge his operations and thereby sell more to the United States. As the hon. member knows, very little coal comes out of New Brunswick into other Canadian provinces. When it does it receives subvention assistance, the same as the coal from other provinces. The subvention policy, however, does not extend to the movement of coal within a province, and that condition applies all across Canada. My hon. friend is mistaken when he says that subvention is paid on Nova Scotia coal delivered in New Brunswick; that just does not happen.
If there were a problem in connection with the marketing of New Brunswick coal we should be only too happy to attack that problem and find a solution for it. At the present time the New Brunswick operators seem capable of taking care of themselves and able to find their own market. The industry is in a healthy state.
It is better now than it was.

It is generally conceded that the coal mining business in Canada finds itself in a difficult position. When I heard the hon. member for Macleod refer to diesel engines my mind went back to 1932, at which time, accompanied by a number of operators and the presidents of various local unions, I had the privilege of interviewing the then minister of labour and minister of mines, Mr. Gordon. At that meeting were Sir Edward Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and Sir Henry Thornton, representing the Canadian National. I cannot help recalling a reply I received from Sir Edward. While at that time they had not begun to use diesels, they had begun to use oil in the locomotives moving west from Calgary; indeed, that whole area out to Vancouver became an oil burning division. I remember suggesting to Sir Edward Beatty
Supply-Trade and Commerce that perhaps that should not be done, because it would be a blow to the coal mining industry of western Canada. I have thought many times since just how true his answer was when he said, "Smith, if there is no other answer, it is progress." I believe parliament would be most unwise, in connection with any industry, to do anything to stop progress. We know that things are progressing in other countries with which we may be in competition.
In connection with our excess supplies of coal I would ask the minister whether there has been any actual advance, or any prospect thereof, in utilizing coal supplies for purposes other than fuel. We have heard from Russian propaganda sources that they have been burning their coal underground to create power. I believe it can be presumed that that report was nonsense. I know we have some experimental stations, but would it not be wise to have some set up at the pit mouth? I am not advocating this; I am merely making an inquiry.
In these days when we speak about power we seem to think of nothing but hydro power. It seems strange that in the town of Drum-heller a plant has been operating successfully for a good many years on slack, the cheapest form of all coal mined. Would the minister make a statement as to power production when cheap coal, and perhaps gas, are available, and compare the cost with hydro power? We know it is true that once the water is harnessed the operating expenses are limited.
Will the minister indicate also whether the blow is going to fall on Alberta coal production next Saturday, July 1? I asked a question of the minister on the orders of the day to which he replied with a sound answer, namely, that that was not a matter of government business but rather an arrangement of rates between suppliers and distributors of coal, and that it was something with which the board had nothing to do. He said, however, that the situation was being watched.
My understanding is that there is a subvention of $2.50 paid to the railway companies for the hauling of this coal to the east. On top of that is an agreed rate of, I believe, $8.40. My understanding is that it is the intention of the railways now to resort to the normal rate of around $13. That, of course, would completely end the use of Alberta coal in these eastern sections. I recall having appeared before the railway commission on one occasion-it is now the board of transport commissioners. Our efforts were directed to finding the cost of hauling a ton of coal from Drumheller to North Bay and Toronto. That was at a time when cost

Supply-Trade and Commerce was not a factor in determining railway freight rates. I could not help but be amused. The Canadian National had brought from the United States an employee of the interstate commerce commission who belonged to a new professional classification; he was a railway cost accountant. The interstate commerce commission had begun the business of endeavouring to relate rates charged for the carriage of freight to cost, and I believe that was the first effort to do so on this continent. I will not mention the name of the gentleman, but he was one of the cleverest men I ever examined. I remember his saying that the haul from .western to eastern Canada was a one-way haul and the cars had to go back empty to Alberta. In building up the structure upon which a rate was finally found he charged so much a ton for the extra vibration of the bridges on the line caused by hauling empty cars back to Alberta. I thought that was wonderful cost accounting, but it struck me that they carried the use of figures a long way indeed.
I should like the minister to say something about uses of coal other than for the generation of heat. If he can tell me anything new about the impending fall of the sword on Saturday with respect to Alberta coal, I would be very happy indeed.

As to the question whether any use has been found for coal other than for fuel, I think the answer is that on this continent no alternative use has been found which is economically sound. A good deal of money has been spent on experiments with the gasification of coal underground, and that has proven to be impracticable. Many millions have been spent on hydrogenation plants designed to make gasoline from coal. These have been found enormously expensive to operate, and have been pretty well rejected as impracticable. In my opinion the future of coal lies in keeping in step with progress in the development of the gas turbine. The gas turbine has economic advantages that are considerably better than those of diesel locomotives. Gas turbine engines are being operated in an experimental way today. The Brown Boveri Company of Switzerland is the leader in the development of gas turbine locomotives at the moment. Over the next few years there may be developments in gas turbines which will make them even more economical than diesels. One advantage lies in the faot that powdered coal is a first-class fuel. I think that is the hope for the future of the coal industry so far as railway operation is concerned.
My hon. friend asked whether coal can compete with hydro power as a source of


power. For a steady load the answer is no. To provide for a 100 per cent load factor hydro power will always be cheaper than power produced from coal. Nevertheless, with fluctuating power load, and especially where hydro power can take the base load, steam is often economical and may offer better economy than the enlargement of a hydroelectric installation.
Stand-by plants.

Stand-by plants perhaps, or rather plants used from time to time where expense can be saved when the power is not required. In the southern states you will find that steam is combined with hydro power and used together with resulting high economy.
My hon. friend asked if the blow to the coal mines is going to occur on July 1. The answer is no.
The hon. member for Macleod is very sceptical about the suggestion that the government is watching the situation. However, the government did watch the situation referred to. It intervened in the later stages and was able to persuade the railroads that the western mines should have a chance to adapt themselves to the changed situation. The result is that the present rates are to be continued until March 31 next. That gives the mines some opportunity to meet the changing situation.
The hon. member for Macleod suggested that there has been a drop in production. I know of no drop in production caused by any situation other than fire and flood. The Brazeau colliery plant above ground * was burned and the Cadomin mine was flooded a while ago. That has reduced the production of bituminous coal, but aside from that I know of no mine in the bituminous field that has curtailed production.
Mountain Park has given up its deep seam production.
As I understand the situation that seam is closed because of exhaustion of the seam:
There have been almost 200 men laid off in one mine in the Crowsnest pass.

My hon. friend will understand that domestic coal follows a pattern that means curtailment of operations in the summer months. The reason is that the western domestic coal cannot be stored, and usually moves directly from the mine to the consumer during the burning season.

It is a bituminous mine.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am told that it is a captive mine. It is owned by Consolidated Smelters. The reason it has curtailed production is that the coke ovens at Consolidated are closed down. I do not think the coal board can regulate that situation. It is not a mine that offers coal on the general market. Its coal output is used by Consolidated.
Is there any future for Canadian coal in the chemical and plastics field?
The Canadian chemical and plastics market is not one that can consume any large quantities of coal. Even in the United States that is a very limited market.
Do I understand from what the minister has said that there is no improvement in the Fischer-Tropsch process?
No recent improvement.
It is not a practical thing to look forward to at the present time?
That is right.
On account of the cost?
Yes.

I was particularly interested in the observations of the hon. member for Calgary West relating to research in this field. The minister's answer was indeed enlightening. It is my sincere hope that efforts will be continued in the field of research. I represent extensive coal mining areas, including the Brazeau colliery, where a disastrous million dollar fire has put more than 400 men out of work. It is expected they will be out of work for more than six months. When I go among the miners of Alberta I hear constantly expressions of concern as to the future of the coal industry, and as to their own employment. They refer to this matter of research, recognizing what the use of oil and gas may do to future markets for coal from the mines in that area. It is only natural that those miners, who have done nothing else throughout their working lives, should be greatly concerned. I repeat that I hope the research work will be carried on with all possible vigour.
When assistance was granted the coal mining industry of the maritime provinces for purposes of modernization, we gave our wholehearted support. We pointed out, however, that conceivably some assistance might be required by the coal mining industry of the west, and that when it became apparent that such assistance was necessary we trusted the government would be just as anxious to
give that assistance as it was to assist the industry in the maritime provinces. Only recently I was checking figures with respect to Alberta's potential coal reserves, together with information as to the actual development up to the present time. It was astonishing to learn how insignificant, if that is the proper word, the development has been in relation to the potential reserves. The operators assure us there is only one reason why the coal industry of my province has not been more fully developed; it is the insecurity of markets. They feel that if we had a clear-cut national fuel policy there probably would be a great expansion. At the present time they are also faced with high costs in relation to the sale price of their product, and a narrow margin of profit per ton.
We have some very large mining concerns in my province, such as the Brazeau collieries. We also have the small family mines, if we may call them that, where half a dozen persons or less carry on the work. Then we have a middle class group of mines such as those found at Alexo and Saunders, for example, producing what we often refer to as domestic coal. I believe that in this middle group we have reached the point where a certain amount of modernization is necessary if production is to be maintained and increased. So far as I can ascertain, however, at the present time those operators are not prepared to invest the money necessary to improve and expand their mines because the future of the industry is so insecure. I am not certain whether assistance has been made available to the coal mining industry of the west for modernization or in connection with production, and I would ask the minister whether any such assistance is granted at the present time, of course apart from subventions and things of that kind. I hesitate to ask whether any such assistance is contemplated, because the minister might tell me that is a matter of government policy to be announced in due course. Has any assistance been granted at all in the western coal mining field for such purposes as modernization?

None of the mines mentioned
by my hon. friend has asked for assistance.
I did not say they had.

If he will look at the balance
sheets of those particular operations he will find that all are in a very comfortable financial position. There has been no plan for capital assistance for the western mines. It is felt that the economic position of those mines would not warrant the government's inviting expansion of the operation. Obviously it is not wise to stimulate production for which there is no sure market. That would be bad

Supply-Trade and Commerce economics, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree. With fuel oil, produced in the same area, undercutting the price of coal, I believe any western operator would be very unwise to invest more capital to expand his operation at the present time.

I just want to make clear that there is no question of the mines having asked for assistance as yet. In view of what the minister has said, however, it seems to me that research becomes very much more important, and I believe there should be a more concerted effort on the part of the government and the board to secure markets for the product of our Canadian mines.

When we speak of coal, as the minister indicated a moment ago, we must keep in mind the importance of maintaining a great industry. As I think the minister knows, the west is in a more precarious position than any other mining district in Canada, in that we have the close competition of oil, which certainly is going to make an inroad into the coal market. On the other hand the coal mining industry becomes of major importance in any national catastrophe that may come upon us, such as war. We saw what happened during the last war, when our coal mines had to make a supreme effort to help supply the demands of Canada during that emergency. So even if there were no other reason I think we should pay particular attention to that industry.
The minister indicated that the department was keeping its finger on the situation in the maritimes, and expressed the opinion that things were going along fairly well there. In western Canada, however, we have not that assurance, partly because of the production of oil. As the hon. member for Macleod indicated a moment ago, we cannot halt progress; but while no one would endeavour to halt the progress that is being made in the development of oil, it seems to me we must do something to maintain this other major industry. Large numbers of .families are dependent upon coal mining for a livelihood. A moment ago the minister said he did not know of any mines that had been closed down.
I mentioned the domestic mines.
When I was home at Easter the miners had a meeting at which it was stated there were 1,400 unemployed.
There is always a good deal of seasonal unemployment in the mines at this time of year.

But this was a very sudden cut-off. Some of the operators were at that meeting, and they pointed out the difficulty they had in competing with United States


coal. They said they just could not do it. Economically I suppose they were right. If I recall aright, one of the operators went on to indicate the handicap they were under through the lack of assistance to bring their mines up to modern standards of mechanization as has been done in the maritimes. I agree with the statement by the minister a moment ago that it would not be good business to encourage production for which there is no market. I believe the coal board has been doing good work as far as it has gone, but I wondered if through the activities of the coal board we could not give the western industry a little more encouragement in the finding of markets for western coal. A moment ago the minister said the board was keeping in close touch with the situation. I am sure it is, but if the minister could give us a little more definite information about what the coal board is doing to develop a market for western coal, it would be of great assistance and encouragement to those who are engaged in mining in the western part of Canada. What is the board doing, and where is it planning these markets for western coal? Can the minister tell us just a little bit about that, and at least give the western industry some encouragement? Exactly how does the board operate?

The coal board, in short, assists the industry to continue as a prosperous operation. The coal board does not perform miracles. I should be reluctant to say anything at this time that would encourage the western coal industry to believe it has a bright future, because I believe the future is far from bright. This situation arises because of developments in its own province. We shall continue to find markets for coal just as long as we can. After we have bonused, to the extent of $2.50 per ton coal which costs only $3.50 or $4 at the pithead, it becomes cheaper to take the miners on the payroll and pay them directly rather than bonus the coal.

First, Mr. Chairman, I want to give personal recognition to what the minister has done, and recognition to him for his knowledge and grasp of the problems of the coal industry in Canada. I also want to express my confidence in the coal board, and the work it has undertaken although it is not complete. I have special confidence in one of the members of the board, who comes from Nova Scotia, Mr. D. W. Morrison. He has been associated with the coal industry for many years. The citizens of his own town of Glace Bay have shown confidence in him year after year by re-electing him as mayor. His health has been such, though, that he has not been able to

continue. I have had many contacts with him, in delegations he has headed, and as I say, I have great confidence in him. Another man who has been associated with the coal board for many years in Ottawa is Mr. Frank Neate, who gave such great service to the province of Nova Scotia in an effort to put the coal industry on a better basis.
The coal industry is a necessary industry. It is only in time of national emergency that we really appreciate it. In order to keep it operating it has been necessary to grant large subsidies, subventions, and so on. I am glad the minister has recognized that policy whioh was put into effect in the early thirties when this industry was at the lowest point it has ever reached in the history of the country. It was meeting competition from imported coal that was being placed on cars in the United States for as little as fifty cents a ton. At that time the Canadian National was getting coal from its own areas, taken over from the Grand Trunk for as little as eighty and eighty-three cents per ton. Coal was coming into Canada from Great Britain and European points as ballast. At that time surplus electric power was being used under boilers to replace coal. This was electric power which would otherwise not be utilized. There were labour difficulties in those days, but the industry was able to carry on, and is now on a better basis.
I was interested in and concerned with the voluminous report on the coal industry submitted by Mr. Justice Carroll, now the member for Inverness-Richmond. There is a tremendous amount of information in that report, but I do not know that any of the recommendations have been actually carried out. I do not know what has been done. Perhaps the hon. member himself will be able to tell us about that. It has been recognized that the coal industry of this country is necessary, and various governments have so recognized it. The chief problem is finding markets in Canada for this industry which would give it an assured production. Last year the government assisted the industry to the extent of a loan of $10 million. This loan was given for the purpose of putting in improvements, machinery, and so on. I would be interested in having the minister say to what extent this loan has been applied. I understand that $7,500,000 was to be applied to provide machinery for the largest industry in Nova Scotia, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. That left $2,500,000 to provide improvements for the smaller mines in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I should like to know to what extent that money has been allocated, and what is being done. Recently the president of Dominion Coal and Steel
Supply-Trade and Commerce Corporation announced that, in order to enable continuous production during the slack season, the coal mines at Springhill in my constituency were to have a port established on the Atlantic coast. This would enable them to ship thirty miles by rail, and then by water to the larger markets in central Canada. While these subsidies have been quite substantial, there has also been a great saving of United States currency through the production and marketing of coal in Canada which has replaced some of the imported coal. It has not been a disbursement without direct returns to this country.
I do not know that there is much more I can say now. I have a good deal of sympathy for the workmen operating those mines. They have had to struggle for years to build up the position that is now recognized, namely, that they are entitled to the largest wage that can be justified. In the county of Cumberland we have a splendid body of workmen who have proven time after time their capabilities and their desire to do their part in operating the coal mines. The smaller mines in the Joggins, River Hebert and Maccan area do not produce coal with as high B.T.U.'s as the Springhill coal, which has the highest heat units of any coal on the continent, but that area does produce splendid domestic fuel. It could be improved if washing plants were established, and I was hopeful that some of this money, the $2,500,000 applicable to the smaller mines, would be made -available for this purpose.
There is much more I could say with respect to the coal industry and its significance in the economy of Nova Scotia, the difficult years through which it has passed, and its importance to Canada as a whole. We have the assurance of the minister that he will continue to do his part in carrying out this policy.

I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland. He has been supporting the coal industry of Nova Scotia for a great many years. He asked for some information as to the appropriations under the capital loans. There have been only two: to the Dominion Coal Company, a loan of $7,500,000, and to the Avon Coal Company, a loan of $375,000. We have a few additional applications that are being considered at the present time, but those mentioned are the only two loans that have been completed.

May I ask the
minister why the 1949-50 coal report has not been made available to us? The latest one I was able to get was that of the previous year, 1948-49.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The difficulty has been that we cannot get the printing finished. If we are not able to get the printed report tomorrow, we intend to table a typewritten copy.
What is the position of the coal mining industry on Vancouver island, British Columbia? They have their problems too, but I think they are different from the maritime problems.
It is in bad shape. I do not know that I could give any details, but mines in British Columbia are fairly well worked out and the situation is not good.
I notice that the amount of subvention, for both this year and last, is $4,500,000. Can the minister tell us what was actually spent last year of that amount?
The amount is about $3,900,000 -a little more perhaps, but in that vicinity.

May I ask the minister this
question? The statutory vote for subsidy payments is for the purpose, as I understand it, of providing a drawback on imported coal used for metallurgical purposes. Why is there a decrease of $50,000 in that amount? What is the amount of drawback paid now on coal used for metallurgical purposes? Does the drawback apply to Canadian-produced coal as well as to American?

This is a subsidy paid on Canadian coal used in making metallurgical coke. The purpose is to place an industry that uses Canadian coal on at least as favourable a footing as an industry using American coal. The only company to which that subsidy is paid, I believe, is Dosco.
What amount is rebated?
It is 49} cents a ton.

I should like to ask the minister if he would answer my inquiry as to what has been done or is being done to provide a shipping port so that Springhill mines can ship, through the slack season in the summer, to central Canada points by water.

Nothing has been done; but as far as I know, all the coal that is mined at Springhill is moved to market in central Canada. It has been for several years and I think it will continue to be. In other words, we do not intend to permit them to have any slack season.

This was an
announcement made by the president of the company, Mr. Forsyth, within the last few weeks.
I shall be glad to look into the matter.

Item agreed to.

National research council-
451. Salaries and other expenses of the national research council, $9,874,903.

This is the first item for the
national research council. As the minister knows, these estimates have been reviewed by the special committee investigating the work of the research council, and I do not think there was any objection to them. What I should like to suggest to the minister is that he give some consideration to the salaries being paid to the research officers. If he will turn to page 281 of the estimates, at which are to be found the details of these votes, he will find that, apart from the directors and assistant directors, there are only 14 other research officers who are drawing a salary of $6,000 or more, and that there are 587 who are drawing less than that figure. If the salaries are sufficient to attract the best men in the country to this work, then of course there can be no objection to them. But I think it would be worth the minister's while to see whether the salaries, particularly in the middle group, are adequate to keep the best men in the country in this field. Personally I was greatly impressed by what we learned of the work of the staff of the research council, from Dr. Mackenzie down. They are doing a splendid job; they are doing work which is of the utmost importance to a young nation like Canada. Our university graduates seem to take naturally to work of this kind. With our natural resources and our comparatively small population, this research work seems to me to be as important as any other work being done in Canada. I would ask the minister to give some thought to the question whether these salaries are adequate.
A good deal of thought has been given to that subject. I think I can say that the research council does attract the best young men in Canada.
I think that is true now. There is no doubt about that.

My hon. friend perhaps has in mind that the salaries paid do not hold these young men permanently. I think that is a highly desirable situation. The worst thing that could happen to the research council would be for young men to come in there at age twenty and stay there until age sixty. A young man gives splendid work to the research council and in return he obtains splendid training from the research council. I believe it is highly desirable, in the interests of the Canadian economy, that after the young man receives that training and has been there for a few years, he should find a place in industry and continue his work in that field.
I have more in mind the men from thirty-five to fifty who are making a career of the research council work.

Such men are carefully selected, and their salaries are better, we will say, than comparable salaries in universities. We can never compete with industry. If industry needs a man with particular qualifications, it will pay any price that it takes to get the man. For instance-and I am perhaps not telling tales out of school-recently one of the men was offered $25,000 a year plus a favourable retirement plan, but he decided to stay at the research council at a salary less than $10,000. If I give too many particulars, you might place the man. The work does attract first-class men. We think that the range of salaries is adequate to attract the kind of men that it is in the public interest to attract to the work of the research council.
The name of that man should be taken and he should be considered for a position in the cabinet.
I do not know that he would take that job.

I want to ask the minister whether he would say a word as to the co-ordination of effort that there is with other research organizations, for example, with the one in Ontario. I think there is co-ordination, but I should like to know more about it.

The purpose of the national research council was to bring about co-ordination of Canada's research efforts. I believe it is doing just that. Efforts are being made to see that there is a minimum of duplication with other research establishments and with those of the national research council, and also to see that there is no great overlapping of effort between the work of the national research council and the work of private industry. If the field is covered by another agency, that work is not undertaken at the national research council.

Item agreed to.
Atomic energy control board-
*454. Administration expenses of the atomic energy control board, $57,000.

This is the first item for the atomic energy control board. Last year the special committee on atomic energy recommended that steps should be taken to establish a second pile at Chalk River. I cannot tell from this year's estimates whether or not that recommendation is being followed. Can the minister explain, and also at the same time tell us whether there has yet been a
Supply-Trade and Commerce decision reached by Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom concerning the release of more atomic energy data for peacetime purposes? In the report of the atomic energy control board I find a reference to that. Paragraph 10 reads:
At meetings of representatives of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada recommendations were made looking to the wider declassification of fundamental scientific information while maintaining restrictions on publication of technological data that might be of assistance to a potential enemy.
It may be that the representatives of the three countries have decided that this is not the time to make any wider declassification; but will the minister tell us the situation on these two points?

As to the first point, those associated with atomic energy expect to be in a position to recommend to the government the building of a second pile. That recommendation has not been made as yet. I believe that the scientists would give as a reason the fact that they are not quite ready with the design. They are incorporating all the knowledge that has been developed since the first pile was built. While I cannot speak positively, it has been intimated to me that the design is not yet ready. There may be several other factors associated with the projects that are being worked out actively.
As to the declassification of information regarding peacetime application of atomic energy, there has been some, but the complete exchange of information that was hoped for has not been brought about, largely as a result of steps in that direction being interrupted by the Fuchs case.
Is the production of uranium in Canada up to the requirements of the country?
Far beyond the requirements of Canada.
What have been the outside expenditures under this heading up to date?
I have not the exact figure, but the expenditures for capital and for operating to date run about $35 million.

Incidentally I want to remind the minister that with respect to this $35 million, plus the appropriations totalling about $8 million which we are putting through, none of it has been spent in the maritime provinces. Therefore in this as in many other large expenditures the maritimes do not share, and that contributes to their difficulties and their lack of prosperity in relation to certain other parts of Canada.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

In that regard I would remind my hon. friend that considerable expenditure is being made in the maritimes for a new laboratory which it is hoped will be opened in October of this year. I am confident that that regional laboratory will make a decided contribution to the economy of Nova Scotia.

I did not
hear the question asked by the hon. member for Cumberland, but I heard the reply of the minister in reference to the maritimes. I should like to ask a question along that line. Is there a possibility of a regional laboratory being built in Newfoundland, or is there any work being carried on there?

The purpose of the maritime regional laboratory was to serve Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. There is a regional laboratory in the maritimes which will be opened this October; there is a regional laboratory for the prairies, and there is a regional laboratory on the Pacific coast.
They deal with problems that will be helpful to Newfoundland?
Yes.
Will this laboratory be carried on as part of the operations of Dalhousie university?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Atomic energy control board-
456. Operation and maintenance, $6,113,530.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
whether there is any revenue in connection with this project which might be regarded as an offset of this expenditure?
There is a substantial revenue item, but I would rather not discuss it.

Item agreed to.
Canadian Arsenals Limited-
458. Administration and operation of Canadian Arsenals Limited, $2,900,000.

Will the
minister explain the figure of $1,300,000 which is indicated as not required for 1950-51?

Last year the estimates contained an appropriation of $2,900,000 for the operation of the dominion arsenals. The arsenals did not require that appropriation. They actually operated at a profit of about $2,500,000; in other words, the sales of products from the arsenals exceeded the operating costs of the arsenals by about $2,500,000. That was not a normal situation, in that there were certain wartime stocks of raw


materials that were being used up. The surplus stocks in the arsenals were not taken into War Assets Corporation and re-issued; they were left with the arsenals to liquidate, so that the profit of $2,500,000 from the operation of the arsenals is not a normal profit. However, an effort is made to operate the arsenals at least on a break-even basis, and the item that we are asking parliament to vote today is an insurance item rather than an item that will necessarily be expended.

This is one of the cases where the minister's miraculous forecasting worked out. Seriously speaking, it does not look as if it had been a budget at all last year. As the situation worked out, there was a difference of several millions between what was estimated and what was needed.

I am neither a prophet nor a seer. I could not foretell that India, Pakistan, Israel and a few distant countries would come in with large orders for munitions. Had we relied upon our own requirements of munitions for the armed services we would have required the $2,900,000. That is the cost of maintaining the arsenals in a stand-by condition, if there is no work in progress.

I should like to thank the minister for a note he sent me some time ago concerning the arsenal at Lindsay. He said the government would keep it running. The payroll means a good deal to that town. When I saw that this amount of $1,300,000 was not required I wondered if it had anything to do with that plant, but the minister's answer to the hon. member for Greenwood would indicate that that is not so. Shall we continue in the future as we have in the past so far as this arsenal is concerned?

I was asked about the item of $1,300,000 not required this year. That was to replace the fire loss at Quebec arsenal. The hon. member will recall that one of the buildings was destroyed by fire last year. That was a capital vote put in to replace the building, and that is why this amount is not required this year.
Lindsay arsenal has been made an important unit of our arsenals system. It handles the manufacturing of the large*r types of shell cases. Every effort is being made to keep it well supplied with work.

Item agreed to.
Special-
784. To reimburse the Canadian Commercial Corporation for expenses incurred in purchasing materials, supplies and equipment, etc., on behalf of the Department of National Defence, under chapter 51, statutes of 1917; further amount required, $31,736.

Is the construction of 135 housing units at the camp of the Royal Canadian Engineers at Vedder Crossing, British Columbia, being done by Canadian Commercial Corporation or by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?
When was the work undertaken?
I think it is almost completed.

The chances are it was undertaken by Canadian Commercial Corporation. Within the last year it has been the practice to have practically all housing work for the services carried out by the housing corporation. Prior to that, small groups of houses were handled by Canadian Commercial Corporation.
I have had complaints about the construction and the inspection. I suggest that the minister have one of his officers investigate the situation.

269. Departmental administration, $1,373,625.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two brief observations. What I shall say first will, I believe, reflect the views of all hon. members on both sides of the house. May I say to the minister, who has returned to the house after an illness, how pleased we are that he has made such a complete recovery and is with us again in his normal good humour and good health.
On previous occasions I have asked, and I repeat the request now, that a committee be set up to deal with the question of rural mail couriers in Canada. I realize of course that it is too late this session to take that action. I cannot understand why minister after minister has declined to do it.
There may be a disposition on the part of some hon. members to think that the problem of rural mail couriers is an isolated one and does not deserve the attention of,a committee of the house. Nothing could be more remote from the fact, because, as the minister knows, the whole network of mail distribution across the country is of great importance not only to the couriers themselves but to those whom they serve.
Supply-Post Office
The minister is no doubt aware that there have been many criticisms of the manner in which rural mail contracts are let, and I suggest that a committee of the house could study the question and make recommendations so that the mail couriers from coast to coast would get a fair break. Those of us who for many years have been served by the couriers know that their problems should receive more attention than they have received in the last few years. If there are problems, then they should be dealt with by a committee of the house.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Prior to the noon recess I
was calling on the Postmaster General to set up a special committee at the next session of the house to deal with the question of mail delivery by rural mail couriers. I want to add to what I said then the observation that the long history of the rural mail couriers has not been a very happy one, nor is it one for which parliament or the government can take much credit. The rural mail courier renders splendid service. He is an intimate part of the rural life of Canada, but unfortunately the remuneration he has received has been so scandalously out of line with that paid to others performing similar public service that it has called for condemnation by many members on both sides of the house.
I am not going to say that there have not been patchwork reforms aimed at attempting to relieve the position of this public servant. Bonuses have been given and changes made, but the objection is that he is still working under an outmoded system which perpetuates the inequalities under which he labours year in and year out. The association which has the interests of rural mail couriers particularly at heart has called incessantly for a committee of the house to hear witnesses, gather information and allow the employees concerned and others interested in the service to come to Ottawa to present their point of view for the purpose of having the matter thoroughly studied, and if possible the policy revised so that the rural mail courier will get a square deal.
There is another important point that the committee would normally deal with. While the dwellers in rural areas for the most part are provided with service to their gates six days a week, and while city dwellers on paved streets in the larger towns and cities have mail delivery six days a week, there is a vast section of our population which does not come within either of those classifications. With

the housing programs and the extension of residential areas outside of the larger cities and towns, many rural sections have now been transformed into suburban areas with scores of thousands of people living there who used to live in the cities and towns. The difficulty arises from this vast extension and the increase in population in the suburban parts of the country.
In many instances these areas are too thickly populated for the ordinary rural mail route, yet they do not qualify under the regulations for city postal delivery service. I have been wondering what can be done in cases of that kind. I know that the Post Office Department has been making attempts to alleviate the condition. At this point I should like to say that in the representations I make from time to time to the department-and I am sure this is true of other members of the house-I have been met with courtesy and co-operation on the part of the Post Office Department in reference to these urgent and vital problems.
As I see it, the difficulty is that what is needed is a brand new policy as to suburban mail delivery. With a view to being of some assistance to the committee and the department I wrote last November to the Postmaster General of the United States. As a matter of interest and information I want to put on record the letter I received from Mr. Donaldson, their Postmaster General, dated November 10, 1949. It reads:
Dear Mr. Graydon:
This will acknowledge your letter of November 2, 1949, inquiring about the type of service rendered by this department to suburban districts throughout the United States. This department maintains rural delivery service on 32,556 rural routes which serve not only the farm areas of the country but cover many of the highways and roads in the suburban areas of our cities and towns.
When the population in such areas, particularly those adjacent to large cities, becomes congested to the extent that rural delivery service is no longer feasible either from the standpoint of mail volume or frequency of stops, such territory is transferred to the city delivery service and maintained by carriers who are provided with vehicles. This service is provided in territory adjacent to' the well developed city areas but in which sidewalks and other city improvements have not been provided. Where government-owned vehicles are available in postal units that equipment is used and in other cases where the government-owned trucks are not available, the carrier serving such a route is granted an allowance under contract for providing a privately-owned vehicle.
I am sure you understand that under our laws and regulations we maintain city .delivery service in about 4,400 cities where the delivery work is accomplished by carriers on foot. This service is maintained in cities under authority of law which requires that such service be maintained at every incorporated city, village, or borough containing a population of 50,000 within its corporate limits, and may be established at every place containing a population of not less than 10,000 within its cor-
IMr. Graydon.]
porate limits, or at any post office which produces a gross revenue of not less than $10,000 per annum.
The department follows a policy of withholding the establishment of city delivery service, either by foot carrier or mounted carrier, in communities having less than 2,500 population, even though the receipts of the office meet the minimum requirements of $10,000. Carriers in the rural delivery service sell stamps, accept parcels for mailing, register mail for the senders, and also accept applications and money for the purchase of money orders. City delivery carriers, whether on foot delivery routes or mounted routes, do not render such service to the patrons.
With every good wish, X am,
Sincerely yours,
J. M. Donaldson Postmaster General
As the minister will see from this letter, the problem of suburban mail delivery has been tackled with vigour and considerable effectiveness by the Post Office Department at Washington. If the Postmaster General would go into the southern end of my riding, or the suburban portions of other ridings, he would see a striking example of inconvenience and inefficiency with respect to mail delivery. That inconvenience and inefficiency are not occasioned by the quality of the service the rural mail courier tries to perform; they result from the fact that the system is not right. At one point in my own riding where there are perhaps fifty or sixty mail boxes, the last report I had indicated that the mail courier had no less than 465 stopping points. In addition we must remember that the danger on the highway is very great. In some suburban areas you can see almost a forest of mail boxes, extending perhaps a hundred yards along the highway. These involve considerable danger, not only because the mail vehicle has to stop so often on the highway, but also because many children have to cross the highway in order to collect the mail, having come a considerable distance from their homes in order to do so. Only this morning I had a letter from one of my constituents who said that having left Toronto and come to my riding to live, the nearest point at which he can get mail is a mile and a half away; and that situation could be duplicated thousands of times all across the dominion.	,
I suggest to the minister that this problem has assumed most serious proportions, and that it is daily becoming more aggravated because the building program is going ahead rapidly. Every time a new house is built the problem becomes worse. It seems to me that the whole matter of rural mail delivery, including the letting of contracts and the very low salaries which in the past have been paid rural mail couriers, ought to be dealt with by a parliamentary committee. The rural mail problem has never been given a

real going over by a committee of this house, though we have dealt with many other things that no doubt were important. Let us not forget, however, that these are the things that touch the home life of every rural community in Canada. We cannot simply sit here and discuss in a general way, toward the end of the session, matters so important in the lives of the people in our rural communities, and let it go at that. From time to time we have had committees to deal with matters which in my opinion have not affected the rural life of this country to anything like the extent it is affected by our mail delivery, and I believe it is time we gave that consideration to this problem.
Today I rose only to make what I hope have been constructive suggestions, because I do not believe there is any point in trying to be unduly critical of anyone in connection with this matter. It is a situation that has developed over the years. .If criticism should be offered, I think it would be that the department has not pursued the matter with the vigour which I believe our expanding suburban population have a right to expect.
I ask the minister, as I have asked him before and as I hope I do not have to ask him again, to set up a committee to deal with postal delivery service in Canada, a matter which affects the lives', the happiness, the convenience and the accommodation of people in the rural portions of this country.

Before the minister replies I should like to say that I agree with what the hon. member for Peel has said, with the exception of his conclusion.
At the outset the hon. member made a courteous reference to the return of the minister. Everyone is pleased that he has returned in good health and is able to carry on the heavy work of his department. During his absence the acting minister was the Solicitor General, who did a very good job.
I am very much interested in the matter of rural mail delivery, and most of the remarks of the hon. member for Peel were to the point. It is my experience that rural mail delivery renders a great service to rural communities, but sometimes a contractor makes a low bid in order to obtain a government contract, which he frames and puts in his drawing room as though it were a Ph.D. degree or something of the sort. They put in the lowest bids, in the hope that their members of parliament will see to it later that the amounts stipulated in the contracts are increased. They want the contracts under any conditions; and those who make bids that are too low can blame no one but themselves if they are not well paid.

On the other hand it very often happens that the officials of the department are stingy in dealing with the tenders. They do not know the geographical conditions; they do not know whether there are steep hills or whether the road is level, and they have established an average which is the same for a mountainous countryside as for a plain. The member of parliament is the one who knows best, and his suggestions as to a fair price for a service should be listened to. In the past it was the custom of the officials to ask tenderers to reduce their prices. In my humble view, when a tender is called for there should be no bargaining afterward. The contract should be given to the lowest tenderer, if he has the equipment with which to do the work. Sometimes there is some merchandising, some auctioneering by the officials of the communications branch. They think the tender is too high, and they ask him to bring it down and down until it reaches a point where it is no longer a paying proposition. In my humble opinion a man who bids for a mail contract should be allowed enough to pay him a legitimate salary, and to cover his expenses. No man is supposed to make a sacrifice to carry the mail anywhere in Canada. I would be interested in knowing the average price per mile paid to mail carriers in each province in Canada. I presume that in Quebec it is lower than anywhere else.
Higher.

No; I may be wrong, but it is my contention that the price the Post Office Department accepts in the province of Quebec is lower than anywhere else. I well remember the fight I had to try to have a fair price paid for mail service in a mountainous countryside. I am glad to tell the minister that conditions are now much better than they were under his predecessor. My post office, and rural route No. 5, are not so thick and heavy as they were under his illustrious predecessor. I had to write letter after letter to try to get an answer, and it was always the same. If the present incumbent were not in charge of the post office, I would vote to reduce the estimate to $1 because I had no satisfaction before he took charge. Conditions have improved, and I thank the minister for that.
I should like to ask the minister when mail delivery service will be established in the city of Riviere du Loup. I hope it will be done soon. Yesterday I was told that an order in council was required for that purpose. Everyone is in favour of it, and I expect the minister to establish it at the earliest possible opportunity. I should also like him to establish a rural route in the
