parish of St. Patrick, Riviere du Loup, to the east of the present post office, to serve that rural community. It could be easily done. In the first place the petition was not understood but I hope it is now, and the farmers who live in that part of my constituency will enjoy rural mail delivery service in the near future. I thank the minister for having established many new rural routes in my constituency. I do not understand why at times it is so difficult to have these routes established. Naturally, there are geographical difficulties, and there may be some argument about the price asked, or there may be some divergence of opinion in the community, but as a rule all the people who do business want to have their mail as soon as possible. It is not the same today as it was fifty years ago. The amount of mail has increased, and it makes quite a difference to the rural mail carrier. He has to buy a bigger truck to handle all the material, and that means greater expense.
In conclusion, my hon. friend asked for the establishment of a committee to study the case of the rural mail carrier. I do not think that is necessary at all, and I shall tell him why. It is for this reason I wanted to speak before the minister. During the war we established a system of adjustments for mail carriers who had more mail, more parcels, newspapers and so on, to carry. By virtue of an act that was passed by parliament, a bonus was allowed. The minister dealt with the mail carriers fairly; even the predecessor to the present minister was quite fair, but more argument was needed to get results from him. The matter was handled fairly without any political partisanship, and an adjustment was made so that the mail carriers would have a fair deal. We have the example of the past, and judging by the revenues of the Post Office Department, which are as large as they were during the war, we have as much mail passing through the office as we had during the war. If that legislation was good during the war, because of the increase in correspondence at that time, I do not see why the same legislation is not used again. This would ensure that the mail carrier who has more mail to carry now than he had before would have an opportunity for righting the wrong he is suffering. I am in favour of a fair deal. After that legislation is re-enacted we might adopt the suggestion of the member for Peel. If that legislation did not work so well in the future as it has in the past, then we might have a committee of the house to study the matter.
I have been here longer than my hon. friend. I remember a time when Mr. Anderson was the superintendent of mail service, and there was a fellow who was asking the
.[Mr. Pouliot.l
mail couriers to contribute some money for an organization to increase the price paid to mail couriers. It was pure humbug, and I do not know what happened to the fellow but nothing was done to help the mail couriers until remedial legislation was introduced. This legislation gave everyone a fair chance. In conclusion, sir, I should like to say to my hon. friend that I am not in favour of a committee. We have enough committees. We have committees for this and that. The members are never in the house because they are sitting on committees. They are listening to what this expert says. We do not need an expert. When the minister suggested that the officials of the department should explain the functions of the Post Office Department to hon. members, I told him we did not need those officials to give lectures to members of parliament. We know what is going on in the Post Office Department. The only thing the minister needs to do is to tell his officials that they are to be fair with the members of parliament, to respect them and not inaugurate any new, complicated system for efficiency. Some foolish people think only of efficiency. If I want this to be sent to the member across the way, I call a page and he takes it there. An efficient method would be scientific. It would be a new world. Do not pay any attention to the new world. I say that to the minister. Do not pay any attention to superefficiency: just pay attention to efficiency. That is enough for me and I think it is enough for everybody.

At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for Peel and the hon. member for Temiscouata for their kind words. The committee may be sure that I am pleased to bd back. As a matter of fact, if I had listened only to myself I would have been back much e rlier because I was eager to be here. But unfortunately there was a watchdog, in this case my doctor, who prevented me from being here sooner. I wish to thank the Solicitor General for the wonderful work he did while I was away. It has even been suggested to me that I should have stayed away a little longer because people were getting along with him so well. At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I should like to put on the record certain facts dealing with the post office and its activities during the year. This is the first time that the gross postal revenues of the postal service have exceeded $100 million. The figure for the fiscal year 1949-50 is $101,277,435, an alltime high. Part of the increase is accounted for by the fact that this is the first fiscal year in which the revenues have been included from Newfoundland. The actual amount of revenue from that province during

the fiscal year was $1,023,693 and the expenditures on postal service for the same period was $1,532,363. The estimates for the fiscal year 1950-51 which are now presented provide for an increase of $2,087,780 over the fiscal year which ended on March 31.
The main item of increase is for salaries and allowances of employees which amount to $3,455,014. This increase is due in part to additional employees necessary to give service and also to increases in salary rates recommended by the civil service commission and approved by the governor in council. On other items there is a decrease in the amount asked for. During the past year 50 post offices have been raised from a revenue to a staff post office rank. This means that staffs of offices are put on a more stable basis. The employees are classified as civil servants and will enjoy civil service rates of pay and be eligible for the benefits of superannuation.
Letter carrier delivery service has been inaugurated at five points during the fiscal year 1949-50 and door-to-door delivery is in contemplation at approximately 13 different points during the present fiscal year. There has been a decided improvement in the transportation of international mails. This is due in great part to the return to the merchant service of ships which were formerly on war service which have now been reconditioned and placed back into service and also a number of entirely new vessels have been added.
Steady progress has been made in the field of international air mail. At the present time almost half the letter mail between Canada and Great Britain travels by air. This volume of mail which amounts to approximately 240,000 pounds annually is transported almost entirely by Trans-Canada Air Lines. There has been a sharp reduction in the number of parcels sent to Great Britain and other European countries. This reduction is almost entirely in the food parcel category. In 1947 the weight of parcel post carried was 27 million pounds. In the calendar year 1949 the weight carried was 22 million pounds, a reduction of 5 million pounds. This is due in great part to improvement in living conditions in European countries and also to the establishment of special agencies whose mission it is to dispatch food and other supplies to those countries where these necessities are in short supply.
Of the total estimates presented amounting to $85,674,757, 55-96 per cent, or in figures $47,946,100, is for the payment of salaries and allowances. The next large item is for transportation which accounts for 38-42 per cent

or a figure of $32,910,747; 94-38 per cent of the post office expenditures being for salaries and transportation. Supplies, equipment and miscellaneous expenditures make up the balance.
In the realm of transportation there does not seem to be any immediate prospect of price reduction. As a matter of fact, the railway companies have made a request for a drastic increase in mail pay rates. The department feels that the increase requested is excessive and the matter is now under consideration. Pending final decision, payments are being made to the railways at the former rates. Any substantial increases granted will turn the small surplus for the fiscal year 1949-50 into a deficit. We have continued to give air mail service in Canada on an all-up basis. The volume of such traffic increased gradually within the year but is still within the estimates on which the experimental rates of payment were calculated. Payment to Trans-Canada Air Lines for this transportation continues to be made on the experimental basis pending agreement at a regular contract rate. We are hoping that the company will be able to agree to rates which will permit the continuance of the all-up scheme as a permanent feature.
The powers to grant supplemental payments to mail contractors ended on March 31, 1949. Supplements granted prior to that date have been continued for the term of the respective contracts. New contracts established as a result of tenders continue at fairly high rates, and there is no visible sign of any decrease in prices.
The money order and savings bank service continues to grow. During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1950, the number of money orders issued and paid shows an increase of 2-35 per cent over the previous fiscal year. There likewise has been an increase in the number of savings bank deposits.
In the realm of new service, consideration has been given to the establishment of an air mail service for parcel post and printed matter, but investigations so far indicate that there is not sufficient demand to justify such a service in the domestic field. The same situation applies in the international sphere. However, the situation is one which is being closely watched and when it is felt that worth-while advantages would be gained the service will be introduced.
In 1949 a departmental committee was established to examine all printed forms and other types of stationery used in the department. This committee has met and still meets regularly and, ns a result of its operations,

Supply-Post Office
there has been a sharp decrease in the number of forms used, which has not only added to the efficient operation of the service but has resulted in worth-while economies.
The department has continued its program of training employees and arranging exchanges between the operating and headquarters services with beneficial results. We have also placed at the service of the mailing public a group of public relations officers who not only explain the facilities which the department offers but help the various mailers with their individual postal problems.
We are continually studying ways and means of improving service and effecting economies. There is under consideration at the present time the experimental installation of a mechanical sorting machine. This machine has been used effectively in other administrations, and we feel it can be adapted to the Canadian service with savings in manpower and improved working conditions.
The . improvements so far made have increased the output of each employee by approximately 6-6 per cent over the last five years.
The growth of the service to its present structure with an increase in postal revenue, year by year, to an all-time high of $101,277,435.43, has always been marked by a judicious combination of the best in traditional postal experience and the adoption of new ideas and modern procedure in its administration and organization. The result is that today the Canadian postal service ranks with the best to be found in any country in the world.
During the fiscal year 1949-50 its activities were as follows: it carried 1,365,492,384 letters and postcards; 612,000,000 newspapers; 790,912,000 pieces of printed matter. Through its money order system it handled $479 million -I am leaving out the thousands-in money order transactions.
How many people have you counting these letters?

It is automatic. It encouraged thrift in its savings bank system to the extent of $38,754,000. It carried goods to the extent of 69,201,000 parcels; it operated an insurance system insuring 225,000 parcels. In its c.o.d. system it handled over 8,364,000 c.o.d. articles. It provided a registration system handling 18,500,000 orders. It gave rural delivery to 368,758 rural boxholders. It operated 57 air mail services with a total route mileage of 29,095 miles.
The number of employees required to operate and maintain the Canadian postal
[Mr. Kir.fret.J
service at its present high level of efficiency is approximately 46,000, which is approximately one-third of the civil servants serving the country. This covers staffs at headquarters in Ottawa, the operating service in the field, the revenue postmasters and their assistants, and mail contractors.
This is a brief statement of what has been accomplished during the past fiscal year. I cannot let this occasion go by without expressing my appreciation of the loyal and efficient service given by the employees of the department generally in their desire to continue to make the postal service of Canada the best of all.
On the question of mail couriers, the hon. member for Peel said that we pay salaries scandalously out of proportion to other salaries. The first remark I would make is that it is not a salary because all rural mails are carried on tender. If I may answer the hon. member for Temiscouata at the same time, I would say that the very considerations that he himself gave with reference to the various hills or conditions of the land make it practically impossible for us in the department to fix a uniform salary throughout Canada, or even to establish any sort of zone where salaries could be paid. We feel -and I think we are correct in this assertion -that the rural couriers themselves when they are making their tenders know the conditions of their land much better than anybody else, and that that should determine the prices that should be paid per mile in the various areas.
In this connection I might say that the average price per mile paid to the rural mail couriers since 1939 has increased by 65 5 per cent, which I think corresponds to the increase in the cost of living, and also corresponds to the increase that has been given other civil servants.
The minister thinks they are getting enough?

I am not in a position to answer that. They themselves fix the amount that they are to receive, because they are the ones who make the tenders. If at the present time a courier feels that he is not receiving sufficient for the services he is performing he has the right under his contract to give three months' notice to the department, and the department will have to call for tenders. If the amount that is actually paid is not met by a smaller tender, or if the tenders for similar service are higher, the department will have to accept the higher tender unless they can get a reduction in it.

May I ask the minister this one question? Why should they be singled

out as the only branch of the public service that must have their jobs given by tender?

It is not a job that they are performing; it is a contract that they have with the government. I know of no contract that is given by the government except by tender. In 1939 the average cost per mile per annum-that is a daily frequency-was $32.35. In 1950 it had gone up to $53.55, which, as I have just said, equals an increase of 65.5 per cent. May I at this time answer the hon. member for Temiscouata. The price per mile throughout Canada is as follows. Unfortunately I cannot give him the information by provinces, but I will give it to him by district. In Vancouver the average cost per mile, based on a service of six times per week, was $71.53, which represented a cost per box per annum of $7.43. As I continue I shall give the two figures that represent these two things. At Edmonton, $60.41, and $14.18; Calgary, $56.48 and $14.96; Saskatoon, $60.02 and $16.38; Moose Jaw, $62.36 and $16.72; Winnipeg, $60.08, and $14.67; London, $52.27 and $13.21; Toronto, $54.49 and $12.84; North Bay, $57.92 and $19.27; Ottawa, $49.44 and $17.49; Montreal, $51.72 and $15.25; Quebec, $52.77 and $16.87; Saint John, $51.45 and $19.68; Halifax, $55.54 and $18.33 and Charlottetown, $53.18 and $17.07. As I have already pointed out, that represents service to 368,758 rural box-holders. It represents a daily mileage of 101,452.5 miles.
On the question of rural mail, I know that my hon. friend is very much interested. We have a long-range plan that we are working on, but we feel that by putting it in operation too soon we would disrupt the service as it is at the present time.
We have more than 5,000 rural routes at the present time. Those must be permitted to operate, and we find it necessary to make changes from time to time.
Is the minister considering inaugurating a system similar to that which has been introduced in the United States?

I was about to deal with that question. In the matter of suburban delivery one must always keep in mind density of population. I am not ready to follow all the practices in use in the United States, one of the chief reasons being that at the close of last year they showed a deficit of $551 million. I think therefore that if we were to put into operation all their practices-I shall not call them schemes-we might find ourselves in a bad financial position.
We are considering however the possibility of giving added service to suburban areas. We have our regulations which must be

followed. The difficulty is that there is always a limit as to the points on the outside of villages, towns or cities, which can be served. At what point are we to stop? If we stop at one place we will find some person perhaps only 75 or 100 yards farther on who would want the service. If we agree to give that service, then we will find another one perhaps another hundred yards farther on who will expect to have delivery.
For these reasons standards have been established. The distance, for two deliveries per day, is up to twenty yards; for one delivery it is between twenty and forty yards; and, generally speaking, over forty yards delivery is not warranted. But that is a city rather than a suburban delivery service.

As a city grows the suburban areas are taken in. As I said earlier, we are considering another plan at the present time. However, it has not yet been advanced to the stage where I can give any particulars with respect to it. This very point has been considered, because we feel that this may be one place where our service is not quite equal to our usual standard.
The hon. member for Temiscouata asked when the service in Riviere du Loup is to be inaugurated. That is one point where it is possible a service may be established this year. In order to obtain letter carrier service we have established certain standards. The first of these is that there must be at least two thousand points of call, and the postal revenue collected must be more than $35,000. Walking conditions must be good, and there are certain other conditions which must be complied with. As soon as the Various centres on the verge of becoming letter carrier centres meet these conditions we will give the service to them.
The hon. member for Temiscouata also referred to the bonus which, until March 31 of last year, was given under the legislation. To my mind this legislation was tantamount to giving to the Postmaster General complete discretion in respect of each of the rural contracts in this country. I do not believe that is what the House of Commons would want.
When about fifty years ago the system was established of giving full discretion to the Postmaster General in all mail contracts below $200, that represented about 87-6 per cent of the contracts. Today, however, that $200 represents only 17-6 per cent of the contracts. That legislation under which the Postmaster General was given full discretion gave him authority, not only over the 17 6 per cent,

but over 100 per cent of the contracts. I am sure hon. members would not be prepared to accept that.

When the bonus system was inaugurated one of the weaknesses was that, unless a rural mail courier knew about the legislation and made application for the benefits thereunder, he was forgotten. In my own constituency I wrote to all the rural mail couriers telling them about the legislation, and in this manner they were informed. I am not sure that was done throughout the country, however. Mr. Chairman, I should like to open my remarks this afternoon in the same way as did the hon. member for Peel prior to the noon adjournment, by expressing my personal pleasure at seeing the Postmaster General back in his place in the house, and looking the picture of health. It is a pleasure indeed to welcome him back to his post and to his duties.
The Postmaster General has just concluded his remarks on one subject concerning the administration of his department by what I thought were commendable references to the undesirability of extended discretionary authority in him as Postmaster General. I could not ask for a better theme for the few remarks I am about to make.
May I say at the outset that I am directing my remarks to the principle involved in a subject that has been dealt with on several occasions during the present session. One recalls the discussions on April 18, May 9, May 16 and May 24. I participated in the discussions on two of those occasions. Today I do hot propose to traverse the ground covered on those occasions, but so far as possible shall focus attention on the principle involved in the exercise by the Postmaster General or officials of his department of powers conferred upon the Postmaster General by section 7 of the Post Office Act.
We are told that the powers conferred by this section upon the Postmaster General go

back to 1889 in their origin, that they have not been changed since, and that the powers thus conferred are widely used. We are told, for instance, that there are about 1,100 orders outstanding at the present time denying the use of the mails to persons in Canada. Only yesterday an instance was brought to our attention where this power was exercised in the case of the Calgary Stampeders, where they and certain persons associated with them have been denied the use of the mails.
The powers conferred by section 7 Cd) empower the Postmaster General, subject to the provisions of the act, to make regulations declaring what shall and what shall not be deemed to be mailable matter for the purposes of the act. Then there are certain direct instances cited and we have these important words:
. . . and for marking on the covering of letters, circulars or other mailable matter suspected to concern illegal lotteries, so-called gift concerts, or other illegal enterprises of like character, offering prizes, or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mailable matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, a warning that they are suspected to be of a fraudulent character and for returning such letters, circulars or other mailable matter to the senders.
I invite the attention of the committee to one fact that seems to me to be of fundamental importance in the interpretation of this section. It is the emphasis placed upon the words "fraud" and "fraudulent". The section does not simply stop with a reference to such things as illegal lotteries and so-called gift concerts. It goes on to refer to "other illegal enterprises of like character, offering prizes, or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public, for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences." In the concluding words it is made clear that this applies "whether the letters, circulars or other mailable matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada," and that power is given to attach a warning that these are suspected to be of a fraudulent character. It is quite clear, sir, that the power is intended to be confined to use in cases where fraud exists or is, on reasonable grounds, suspected to exist, and in the latter case a warning that the contents are suspected to be of a fraudulent character may be given by the marking of certain words on the envelope.
It seems to me that in the interpretation of this power, and of regulations 204 and 206 passed under the authority of the act, sight has been lost of the fact that it is only in cases where fraud exists, or the scheme that is suspected is of a fraudulent character or designed to deceive or defraud the public for

the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, that the power was intended to permit refusal of the use of the mails to any person. Section 204 of the regulations passed under the act largely repeats the language I have just read from section 7(d). Again the emphasis is placed upon the word "fraudulent". The regulation adds:
... it is hereby declared that no letters, packet, parcel, newspaper, book or other thing, sent or sought to be sent through the post office by or on behalf of or to or on behalf of such person shall be deemed mailable matter.
Section 206 of the regulations is declaratory in its nature. It provides:
The Postmaster General has power, under the statute, to mark or cause to be marked upon the covers of letters, circulars or other mail matter suspected to concern schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences, whether such letters, circulars or other mail matter are addressed to or received by mail from places within or without Canada, "suspected to be of a fraudulent character"-
That quotation is taken from the words of section 7(d). Then it proceeds:
-and to return such letters, circulars or other mail matter to the senders.
The Postmaster General's department has attempted to exercise this power in cases where no fraud existed or could by any stretch of the imagination be suspected. The case I referred to on an earlier occasion was one in which the Leaside Lions club, a highly reputable organization, was conducting a raffle as part of a money-rais'ing effort to assist the Manitoba flood relief fund. On that occasion the Postmaster General's department, regardless of the worthiness of the cause, regardless of the fact that the police in the area had been made aware of the fact that lucky number prizes were being offered in this way and that tickets were being sold, stepped in and denied the use of the mails to the club and to the chairman of the committee in charge of the raffle for the club. The ban affected -his personal mail as well as mail received by him on behalf of the club. The Post Office went so far as to return mail in which his own pay cheque was being received from his employer.
Shame.

When the power is exercised or attempted to be exercised in a case of that kind, where there can be not even the slightest suspicion attached to those concerned and no suggestion whatsoever of the scheme being fraudulent or intended to deceive the public, then I think two facts are laid bare before the house. The first is that the Postmaster General's department is undertaking to use this power in cases where the statute 55946-266

does not authorize it, and in the second' place, this legislation must be brought under review by the House of Commons.
We have courts to deal with offences against the criminal law. We have a considerable volume of criminal law in this country. Surely it is not the intention of the House of Commons, in carrying forward on the statute books the Criminal Code and legislation of a similar nature, to leave it to a department to step in and create criminal law, or to set itself up as a body that assumes the function of filling in any gaps that may have been left in the criminal law enacted by the parliament of Canada. That never was and never could have been the intention of parliament in 1889 in enacting section 7(d) of the act. If there are gaps in the criminal law today it is the duty of the government, and particularly of the Minister of Justice, to bring legislation before the house to be enacted for the purpose of filling the gaps in the criminal law, but it should not be left to officials of a department to create law or to take upon themselves the function of the parliament of Canada.
On the question of enforcement, with all respect to the officials of the Department of the Postmaster General, it seems to me that in the case I mentioned-and there must be many others like it such as that of the Calgary Stampeders mentioned yesterday- the matter of law enforcement could very well be left to the law enforcement officers of the area concerned. There are efficient law enforcement authorities in these areas without requiring some special supplement by officials at Ottawa in a department whose principal concern is not the enforcement of the criminal law. The instances I have cited cannot be said to be in any way similar to the case conjured up by the Minister of Justice on a previous occasion during the present session where the offence involved the purchase and sale of securities and he contended it was not covered by the provincial law. Here is a situation which may have been a lottery but certainly could not be said to involve any wilfully illegal lottery, and by no further stretch of the imagination could be said to involve any attempt to deceive or defraud the public.
I think great care must be taken by the post office authorities in lottery cases. I do not propose here today to discuss whether lotteries are right or wrong. I suspect that the view I entertain on the subject of lotteries per se would not be any broader than the view of the Postmaster General, but not every lottery is illegal under the Criminal Code. Section 236 of the Criminal Code, while making certain games of chance and lotteries illegal and attaching penalties for

breaches of the law, goes on in subsection 6 to provide that the section does not apply to a considerable list of things, five in all, which otherwise obviously would fall within the definition appearing earlier in the section; and included in that list is the following:
6. This section does not apply to
(b) raffles for prizes of small value at any bazaar held for any charitable or religious object, if permission to hold the same has been obtained from the city or other municipal council, or from the mayor, reeve or other chief officer of the city, town or other municipality, wherein such bazaar is held, and the articles raffled for thereat have first been offered for sale and none of them are of a value exceeding fifty dollars.
I do not say that in the case of the raffle conducted by the Leaside Lions club the prize was not worth more than $50, but I cite this section of the act to lay emphasis upon the fact that not every lottery is illegal under the Criminal Code, and that in any case not every illegal lottery gives the minister occasion to exercise power under section 7 (d) of the Post Office Act. It is only in cases where it is part of a scheme to defraud or deceive the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences that power is given to ban the use of mails.
On an earlier occasion during this session we heard an interesting discussion by the Minister of Justice with respect to the discretion conferred by this section upon the Postmaster General. I regret that the Minister of Justice is not here now, because I should have liked to address these remarks rather directly to him. He sought to place before the house the argument that this was not a power that could be exercised capriciously by the Postmaster General; that if his use of power was arbitrary or capricious it was open to any person aggrieved to resort to the courts in an action against the Postmaster General. I have read the case to which the Minister of Justice referred on that occasion in support of his argument. I cannot find that it lends any colour or justification to his argument. It is well established law, of course, that any public officer who exceeds the authority conferred by any act is liable to an action in the courts by any person aggrieved by that act, so far as it is not justified or authorized by statute; but that is very different from saying that if the Potsmaster General confines himself to his statutory powers, yet exercises those powers in a capricious or unreasonable way, any person can bring action against him. The decision referred to falls far short of laying down any such proposition. The case is Literary Recreations Limited v. Sauve and Murray, reported in 58 Canadian Criminal Cases at page 385. This was a decision in

1932 of the Court of Appeal of British Columbia, and the headnote reads:
Under the Post Office Act . . . and the regulations made thereunder, the Postmaster General of Canada has the right to determine what is "mailable matter" and has a discretion to prohibit the use of the mails for the sending of non-mailable matter, and his discretion is not open to review by a court.
One would have thought that was very clear, but if the Minister of Justice still persists in an unsound argument I invite his attention to the language used by Mr. Justice McPhillips at page 391, where the learned justice refers to parliament and deals with this very section 7(d) of the act and regulations 204 and 206. He had this to say:
The legislature having clothed the Postmaster General with these extreme powers-
I pause there to draw attention to this very apt description applied to these powers by the learned justice of appeal.
-but I have no doubt proper powers concerning the question of peace, order and good government -it is not within the province of a court of justice to say what is the reasonable use of the conferred powers granted by statute. That is to say tile discretion given by statute to the Postmaster General is an unfettered discretion to determine what shall and what shall not be deemed to be mailable matter.
In my humble submission the matter could not be put more clearly. The court there is saying that the discretion conferred upon the Postmaster General by section 7(d) is an unfettered discretion, and no court has the power to review the exercise of that discretion or to say whether it is reasonable or unreasonable. It is only when the Postmaster General goes completely outside those powers that any person aggrieved by his act has a right against him in the courts. So, Mr. Chairman, I submit to the committee that the argument addressed to the house on a recent occasion by the Minister of Justice was completely unsound.
I go on from that to this point. This discretion, being unfettered and not open to challenge or review in the courts, is so broad, especially having regard to the striking instances in which it has been exercised of late, that I earnestly submit that this house must assume responsibility for reviewing this legislation. If legislation of this kind is capable of such arbitrary use, if the use of the powers conferred under it is not subject to review by a court, then I submit it is high time this parliament qualified the powers conferred upon the Postmaster General by this act. No official of government, however reputable he may be, or however sound his judgment, has any right to possess powers as sweeping as these without any recourse on the part of those thereby affected to a court

or other body by way of review of his decisions. The rights of people as citizens are being freely interfered with. In the case to which I referred a reputable citizen of the community, engaged in charitable work out of which he was not receiving a cent but to which he was contributing a great deal of time and effort, has his personal mail stopped as well as the mail of the Leaside Lions club, in whose behalf he was engaged in this charitable work. I think it is high time this house took steps to see that this power is not left in the unfettered and untrammelled form in which it seems to exist today.
Therefore I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come when parliament must take the responsibility of limiting this power, making sure that it is not capable of being used in any case where fraud is not involved, and also that where the power is exercised it is subject to review in the courts in a speedy manner. In concluding his remarks on May 16, at page 2534 of Hansard, the minister said something that was very sensible. I believe many of us in this house hoped that the hon. gentleman would follow up the sound views and good intentions he expressed on that occasion by introducing legislation to give effect to them. These were his words:
I do admit, Mr. Speaker, that the remedy presently available to challenge an action-
That is to say, an action by the Postmaster General in the purported exercise of his power under section 7(d).
-if it happens to be arbitrary is a little difficult from the legal standpoint.
Now, it is something to wring a statement like that from the Minister of Justice on an occasion of this kind. He proceeds:
We have been quite frank with this house in saying that the present remedy is not very satisfactory. It may cause a legal delay . . .
May I interject again, sir, to point out that what the Minister of Justice was referring to as the "present remedy" is a remedy that exists only in cases where the Minister of Justice has gone beyond the powers conferred on him by the act. Even in those cases the remedy, according to the Minister of Justice, is admitted to be not very satisfactory. He continues:
It may cause a legal delay, and it may in that way create secondary effects upon the offending person which are out of all proportion to his deserts. The move which we have under consideration, therefore, is that of providing an appeal from the order, and not an obscure appeal or an appeal which will take a long period of time, but a summary appeal. Once an order had been made, the citizen offended could make a quick application to the courts and get the whole matter before a judge, with the power to bring In any relevant evidence which he could adduce in addition to that

which the Postmaster General considered. Then the whole matter could come before the courts in such a way as to completely minimize the harm that would be done to an innocent person.
Mr. Chairman, where is the legislation designed to provide that summary appeal to the courts, the necessity for which was acknowledged by the Minister of Justice when he spoke in this house on May 16? We have waited hopefully for it, and we are now told, in these closing days of the session, that no more legislation is to be introduced at this session of parliament. It must be a matter of very grave regret, Mr. Chairman, on the part of all members of this house who dislike arbitrary powers, and dislike even more the exercise of arbitrary powers where they can be found to exist in the statute books. While the Minister of Justice and the government delay introducing legislation to provide a remedy, which the Minister of Justice admits to be so necessary, the arbitrary use of the power continues. The member for Calgary West has drawn to the attention of the house an incident this week illustrating the further use of this power under arbitrary circumstances. This points even more directly than ever to the necessity for action on the part of parliament to put an end to this arbitrary power; to remove the breadth of this power; and the necessity of providing that powers of this kind, as well as the arbitrary exercise of which they are capable, as we have seen in those cases, in the hands of the Postmaster General's department, are made subject to review by the courts.
In most cases the decision of a judge in the courts is subject to appeal. There are few cases in which we leave a matter to the decision of one man. Even judicial determinations in a judicial tribunal are subject to a right of appeal in all except a relatively few cases. Yet today, from the exercise by an official or the minister of the power conferred upon him by this section, there is no right of appeal. How long can this parliament tolerate the continuance of a situation of that kind, sir? I submit to this parliament that a remedy must be provided of the kind acknowledged by the Minister of Justice to be needed, and shown now by this further exercise of this arbitrary power in an irresponsible way to be so necessary at the present time that it can brook no more delay.

I may say that on this question of the broker-dealers there was a long discussion while I was away and there has been some discussion since I came back. The discussion that took place since I have been back did not take place in this chamber. I had occasion, with the Minister of Justice, to meet the representative of the brokers' association and we discussed with Hon. Mr. McTague the various circumstances surrounding this matter. The Minister of Justice, in his letter of May 2 to Hon. Mr. McTague, indicated that if the broker-dealers organization wished to present a brief on any of the matters under the Post Office Act in which it has an interest, the government would be glad to give such representations most careful and thorough consideration.
The broker-dealers association accepted this offer and a brief was prepared which was presented on behalf of the association by Hon. C. P. McTague on June 12. The Minister of Justice and the Postmaster General represented the government.
As a result of the ensuing discussion, it was agreed that in future, where complaints or information indicated that the mails were being used for fraudulent purposes, before prohibitory action was taken by the Postmaster General the cases would be reviewed by a special board appointed for that purpose. The alleged offenders would have an opportunity of appearing before the board, and would be allowed the services of counsel, if so desired. The board would also be permitted to have the advice of such technical and professional assistance as it might deem advisable. Evidence would be taken under oath.
The board would comprise the following officials: director of administration, chief post office inspector and the departmental solicitor. The place and time of the hearing would be determined by the Postmaster General, and due notice would be given to those concerned. Any costs or expenses in connection therewith incurred by the alleged offenders or those acting in their behalf would be borne entirely by them, irrespective of the eventual finding of the board.

In cases where the board considers that there is evidence to the effect that the person or company has used the mails with intent to deceive or defraud, or to obtain money under false pretences, it shall so be reported to the Postmaster General who, if he finds that there is evidence satisfactory to him that the person or company has used the mails with intent to deceive or defraud, or to obtain money under false pretences, shall thereupon cause to be issued a fraud or prohibitory order denying the use of the mails to the offenders for any such improper purpose.
Initially, the board would be set up and the related procedure formulated and established under the powers vested in the Postmaster General by the Post Office Act, sections 7 (x) and 8.
At a future session the authority could be specifically included in the act itself which is due for revision. This would remove any doubt of the future continuance of the arrangement outlined, and preclude any modification thereof without consent of the house.
The board has been established, and any cases which are now being examined by the department, on the ground that the mails are being improperly used, will be submitted to that board for review in accordance with the procedure herein outlined.
I may say' that this matter has been fully discussed with Hon. Mr. McTague and he agreed as to the procedure that is outlined here, that this protects the interests of the brokers or the interested parties, or at least affords them the opportunity of being heard before the prohibitory order is issued.
Another matter that has been discussed with Mr. McTague is the question of appeal. It was recognized by Mr. McTague that the question of appeal was quite a tricky one and that it would require more time than we had before the end of the session in order to establish the proper procedure to be followed. However, we recognized by these instructions, which have already been given for the constitution of this board, the possibility of an appeal because we want the evidence to be taken under oath and in writing which would form the basis of any possible appeal to a tribunal or other board that might be decided on in the future.
We also discussed with Mr. McTague the possibility of launching criminal prosecutions. While I was away there was discussion in the house to the effect that we had no right to stop the mails of any broker without afterwards launching a prosecution. I have in my

hand-and I am authorized by Mr. McTague to cite it-a letter dated June 16 which reads in part as follows:
I think we are prepared to admit the proposition that the Postmaster General should not be obliged to launch a criminal prosecution. That might be left to his discretion. Some definite provision, however, should be made that a person so convicted of misuse of the mails should have the right to apply to be allowed mail privileges again upon such terms, conditions and undertakings as may be imposed or required by the Postmaster General.
I was not here to hear the leader of the opposition make an objection as far as this was concerned. If it had been our intention to launch criminal proceedings, I would have said that that was the case. Surely he is not going to pretend that we were going to leave this stoppage of mail forever. We have asked those brokers to give us (a) an assurance to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General that in future the offensive literature in question will not be sent through the mails; (b) the company, the shares of which are being offered to the public, will undertake that no literature shall be sent through the mails in connection with the sale of the shares without its approval; (c) the broker dealer will give an unqualified assurance that he will not make any improper use of the mail in future in connection with the issues of shares.

They will have an opportunity to give the evidence that they wish to present. They will have their counsel and all the experts they need. What makes this question of procedure a little tricky is the question of lotteries. The procedure I have outlined touches only the broker-dealers organization. We cannot possibly adopt the same kind of formula procedure in the question of lotteries, because by delaying this procedure before this investigation board the person conducting the lottery could very well keep the mailing facilities until such time as the lottery had been concluded. We do not wish to be in that position, because we want to be able to fulfil the obligation that is ours of protecting the Canadian public.
Reference has been made to the sweeping powers that have been given to the Postmaster General. Well, I think reference should also be made to the very great responsibility that the Postmaster General has of protecting the whole population of Canada, thirteen million people, against some scheming people. I am not saying that every person against whom we stop the mail is a scheming person, but I do say that unless in the process of things we do catch some innocent people we shall soon be faced with a multitude of schemes that will put the population of Canada in very great danger.

I have no intention of entering into any discussion with respect to brokers, honest or dishonest. I agree with what the Postmaster General has said, namely, that where there is fraud we should have wide measures not only to limit but to destroy the means and methods by which these frauds are being perpetrated. But that is not what I have in my mind. On the streets of Ottawa and on the streets of every city in Canada there are motorcars publicly advertising and inviting you to buy a ticket. The sum of money that you pay varies between fifty cents and a dollar, in order that you might have the opportunity of telephoning your wife on a given day and saying: "Wife, you have got a new motor car."
At noon today I bought a ticket for a dollar. It is called "CHML Dream Home." It is for the city of Hamilton flood relief fund. His Worship Mayor Garnet Coulter of Winnipeg will present the dream home in Hamilton on Wednesday, July 5, 1950. This is for the Manitoba flood relief fund. No one is going to tell me that this department is ignorant of what is going on there, and it

has done nothing. Yet when a little football club in which I am interested, and from whom nobody makes any money, puts on a raffle they choose-I will repeat the words-this bureaucratic, arrogant, stupid method of enforcing the wishes of some servant somewhere down the line. What happened?' Every football club in Canada is doing exactly the same thing. It is common knowledge. We all know it. The minister can stand up and say: "I have a regulation here; they are in breach of it." Suppose we are. I do not think we are, but suppose we are. What has happened? Why are we singled out for punishment in this arbitrary and extraordinary manner?
Let him remember, and the people of his department remember, that there are provisions in the Criminal Code whereby persons connected with or conducting lotteries can be punished. Why do they now-I am not worrying about the legal right-in fact step in and usurp the function of every provincial court in the Dominion of Canada? -because our courts are provincial courts. Why do they do it? It is nothing but stupid- slipshod is too mild a word-it is nothing but a stupid move made by some bureaucrats in charge of the business. They need not tell me that the attorney general in any province has not acted. He does not need to act. Anybody who is aggrieved in the Dominion of Canada may sign and swear to an information when he sees wrongdoing, if he has courage enough to sign that information. But that is not the way this is done.
I have no doubt that the Stampeder football club are raffling a car. They have done it every year since I can remember. They have used the mails very, very little. I venture to say that all they have got is some returned tickets, and they have not got one ever sent out by the Stampeder football club. But then they go further. This is what they have done. Mr. T. L. Brook is a friend of mine. He is president of the Stampeder football club. He is a prominent businessman. Talk about czarism; use any word you like! To treat Tom Brook in that way because he happens to be president of the second-best football club in Canada is, it seems to me, carrying the law a tremendous distance. You are making a laughing stock of it when you are carrying it to such absurd lengths. There has been some discussion most certainly in the newspapers, and probably in the house, although I am not sure about it, concerning our franking privilege. I know I am going to say something that will be unpopular with most hon. members. It is this: I personally

am opposed to ourselves and those in the other place being granted the franking privilege, except for our correspondence. I believe that is essential and necessary.
