The answer is no.

I should like to bring a message from the members of my constituency to the Postmaster General. We are pleased to see him able to assume his duties again. I am sure we are all hoping that his health is as good as it would seem to be.
May I pay a compliment or two to those who organize and direct this great service in this dominion. When we think of posting a letter in Vancouver and having it delivered in Halifax without loss or restriction and for the very small sum of four cents, we must be at once aware of the great service thus rendered. If we are willing to pay an additional ten cents we can have it delivered in person, and if we wish to transmit money we can be sure that it will be received without loss. May I commend the staff that carry out the duties and make this great service possible for the people of Canada.
My constituency is located in Upper Canada. Many of its citizens were United Empire Loyalists. The descendants of those people still believe that their representative in parliament is the representative in the House of Commons, and that as such he has duties to perform. Therefore when I mention the great and good work of the department I allow myself to bask in some of the credit.
It is because of accepting some of that credit that I now call the attention of the committee to some of those things which I do not feel reflect credit on the department. Because I am a member representing a constituency I feel it my responsibility to place these facts before the minister.
In my riding I am served by a postman who has carried the mail since 1926. In 1924 he wrote two examinations, one for postal clerk and one for mail carrier. The record of his having tried these examinations appears to have been lost. For a number of years he has performed in an excellent manner, and without loss of time through sickness the duties entrusted to him. For the past four or

five years, whenever there has been a man short in the postal department, this man has been called in to act as clerk, and has been entrusted with the sorting of the mail, the registering of parcels and the selling of stamps. Indeed, he has performed those various tasks which are the duty of any clerk in a post office. I commend the choice of the Postmaster General in permitting this to take place. It has been most fortunate that for perhaps half of the last year he has been permitted to do this work, because during that time he has developed an arthritic spur on his heel and could not possibly carry the mail on his route every day without some days of easier work. It is with great pain that he walks his ten or twelve mile route every day. I quite realize that the civil service regulations are such that unless a man is qualified to hold a certain position he is not entitled to fill it. The record will show that he is not qualified to hold the position although he has been doing the work for the past number of years, by replacing those on sick leave or holidays, in order to assist the operation of the Post Office Department in Guelph. A week or so ago an hon. gentleman in my riding asked me to go for a ride with him around the city. I did so, and eventually I found myself following this mailman who was stepping gingerly on one foot. You could see that without doubt he was in pain every time the foot touched the sidewalk. This hon. gentleman said to me: "If that were a horse and you drove it ten miles every day on a mail route you would likely find yourself in jail."
I should like to point out to the civil service and to the members of the Post Office Department that that is not a humane thing to do. I should like to give a little more of the history of this man, and I hope the committee will bear with me while I do so. He joined a machine gun battalion in 1914 and learned to take apart and reassemble his machine gun in the dark. No papers were required for that. He was in the front lines and was wounded. A piece of shrapnel blasted away a section of his forehead, and he now has a silver plate in place of the original bone that God gave him. He was not questioned whether he had papers to qualify him to perform that duty. As a member whose constituents believe that he should represent them, I put this case before you, and I ask that between the Post Office Department and the civil service commission a slight bit of humanity be displayed, and that a good servant be rewarded in the way he should be.

During the past few weeks I have had a number of protests from people in certain sections of Peterborough city because of the fact that in seven different postal districts deliveries have been cut from two to one per day. The districts now having only one delivery have been enlarged to take in other territory. I do not know the reason for the change but if the minister knows I should like him to tell me what it is. The seven postal mail carriers for these districts have to work six full days a week instead of the usual five and a half days worked by the other twenty-one postal carriers in the Peterborough district.
In addition, the seven carriers covering the districts where there is only one delivery a day have a lot of difficulty in sorting their mail in the post office. I know the deputy minister is aware that the Peterborough post office is an antique. We have been promised a new one since 1913. The seven postal carriers have to use a rope hoist to lift their mail from the ground floor to the second floor. When they have sorted it they have to use the hoist again to lower it to the first floor. As I say, they are working six days a week and the other twenty-one carriers only work five and a half days. I understand the seven working the full six days receive the same pay as the other twenty-one.
The Peterborough post office was built when the population was not more than 10,000. Today the same post office is servicing over 50,000 people. I should like the minister to check not only the question of the districts that have only one delivery a day but also the matter of the hours that these seven men have to work. I had a call from Peterborough the other night about an order in council, I believe it was, having to do with the five day week for civil servants for the summer months. I should like to know whether that applies to mail carriers. I should also like the minister to tell me if he can when the new federal building in Peterborough embodying the post office is to be started. I understand that the requirements have been presented to the Minister of Public Works. We have a new postmaster now. I believe the death of the former postmaster was caused partly as a result of the conditions he had to contend with in the old office. I hope that something can be done to speed up the construction of the new building. If the Postmaster General can say anything about the special features to be incorporated in it I should like him to do so. I understand that Mr. Blackwell, a Peterborough architect, has some of the plans, and I wish the minister would give me any information on that matter that he can. I should also
Supply-Post Office
like to know whether the men who are working six days a week instead of five and a half are allowed overtime. I notice there is an amount of $600,000 in the estimates for overtime.

The answer to the last question is no. We are well aware that there is great need for a post office in Peterborough city, and we are going ahead full steam to replace the present building. So far as the actual construction is concerned, of course you will have to look to the Department of Public Works for information as to that.

What about the one delivery
a day?
I will look into it. When we extend service we have to take this precaution, but I will look into the matter.

The point I am getting at is that we had two deliveries before. Now you have extended the districts, but at the same time you are depriving people of two deliveries who had that service before, which is not right.
I will see what I can do about it.
I know the Postmaster General will agree with me.

Has any effort been made in the past year or two to bring rural postmasters in small post offices under the civil service? I should like to refer to what was said by the hon. member for Kamloops on June 3, 1948, as recorded at page 4775 of Hansard. He said:
I have three or four matters I should like to take up with the Postmaster General. The first is the question raised by the announcement made in the press, and I believe also in the house, to the effect that rural postmasters, or postmasters of small offices, were to be made civil servants. So far as 1 know, the necessary legislation has not gone through the house. Is it intended to introduce a bill this year, or is that to be done by order in council?
The then postmaster general replied:
According to the rules, that is done by the Postmaster General himself. An explanation as to why it is done in that way would take some time, but I would point out that it has always been within the jurisdiction of the Postmaster General.
It is true, as the hon. member says, that a greater amount of post office revenue and a greater number of postmasters are being brought under the civil service, with fair salaries. In the meantime, in respect of post offices with revenue of over $3,000, we are now taking care of rentals ourselves to ensure that we have better places in which to install our post offices. Also, if help is required we see that the salaries of the helpers are fixed by and paid for by the department. The postmaster will have a fixed salary. Postmasters in post offices with revenue of more than $3,000 will, we hope, be eligible for superannuation, if they are not too old. In this way they become permanent employees.

Supply-Post Office
We are working on this matter. A beginning has been made and we hope to be able to continue. It will be remembered, of course, that there are over 12,000 post offices in Canada, and it will take considerable time before we can establish this procedure at every point.
The question I want to ask the Postmaster General now-
All that has been carried out. We have transferred 1,300 in the last two years.

I have a simple question to direct to the Postmaster General arising out of a letter which I found in my box today forwarded by the Canadian peace congress, on which appears the name of Dr. J. G. Endicott. This letter was sent without a stamp, bearing the words "On His Majesty's service," and from what I have heard from time to time the activities of this organization seem to be more or less communistic. I should like to know who are permitted to send letters to members of this house without stamps, on His Majesty's service?
Letters addressed to members of parliament are of course on His Majesty's service.

Perhaps my next question should be directed to the Minister of Justice, but I should like to know whether within the Post Office Department there is any machinery to investigate anything suspicious that may be going through the mail. It is not that I want to cast suspicion on this particular . organization, but I should like to know if there is any machinery to investigate people having suspicious propaganda circulated and give an opinion as to whether they should be permitted to send material through the mail labelled "On His Majesty's service." I am not saying this is communist propaganda, but it seems very queer that letters promoting the Russian way of life should come to us bearing those words.

No one in the Post Office Department, not even the Postmaster General, with the exception of those in the dead letter organization, has any right to open a letter, so there is no way of knowing what is inside it, and therefore no way of knowing whether it contains propaganda, whether good or bad.

I should like to call the attention of the Postmaster General to a matter of great historical importance to his department. Next year Canada will be celebrating the centenary of the issuing of our first postage stamps. Other countries in the world have celebrated their centenaries by holding expositions and issuing special commemorative sets of postage stamps. In 1940, for 
instance, which was Great Britain's centenary, they issued a set of six stamps containing on one side a reproduction of the original Queen Victoria one penny stamp and on the other side a modern picture of King George VI. In the United States in 1947 a special three-cent stamp was issued as well as a souvenir sheet of two stamps containing reproductions of the two original stamps issued (by the United States post office. Within the empire, in the island colony of Mauritius, a set of four commemorative stamps was issued in 1948.
International exhibitions have been held in United States, Switzerland, Belgium, and France, and just last month in London. There is an organization in Canada known as the Canadian association of philatelic exhibitions which is arranging an exposition in Toronto to commemorate this historic occasion, to be held from September 21 to 29, 1951, and I am sure it will be the desire and intention of the Postmaster General and his department to co-operate with this association to the greatest degree possible.
The situation in Canada with regard to the issuing of postage stamps is somewhat different to that in most countries, owing to the fact that before confederation various provinces issued their own stamps. For instance, British Columbia and Vancouver island started issuing postage stamps in 1861, New Brunswick in 1851, Newfoundland in 1857, Nova Scotia in 1851, Prince Edward Island in 1861 and Upper and Lower Canada in 1851. That issue, of course, really marked the beginning of the issuing of Canadian postage stamps. The three prairie provinces never issued stamps. It seems to me it would be very opportune if a special commemorative set were issued in conjunction with this exposition which is to be held in Toronto, which it is hoped will attract visitors from all over the civilized world. Incidentally, stamp collecting is said now to be the most practised hobby in the world.
In issuing these stamps I hope and believe designs can be found which will commemorate the very fine stamps issued by the post office in 1851. I need hardly warn the Postmaster General not to repeat the mistake made by one Charles Connell, who when postmaster general of New Brunswick had a five-cent stamp engraved with his own likeness. That stamp never went into circulation, because the ridicule was so great that he ordered the entire issue destroyed. I know these remarks would not be applicable to the present Postmaster General. I feel confident that he and his officials will take into serious consideration the issuing of appropriate stamps which will bring to the attention of

the world the fact that Canada was one of the first countries to use the postage stamp as a means of prepaying mail.
If I may ask the Postmaster General a further question, what qualifications must be possessed before a postmaster is given consideration as a civil servant?

He must possess the usual qualifications. That is, he must toe well educated and have some experience; and, in offices of more than $3,000, he must pass the examinations of the civil service commission.

A moment ago an hon. member mentioned the question of communist literature being circulated through the mails of Canada. I am not sure that the organization to which he referred admits being a communist organization, so perhaps I need not take it as a case in point. The Postmaster General indicated that no one except officials of the dead letter office has the right to open a letter. I think no member of parliament would want his mail opened, regardless of who was writing to him. I well remember the great protest that arose during the war over the alleged opening of certain letters coming to members of parliament. I fancy that every member would be jealous of his right in that regard. Nevertheless, the hon. member does raise a point which perhaps I might pursue along a slightly different line. If no one except the dead letter office officials has the right to open letters, how is it that the Leaside Lions club, Calgary Stampeders, and such organizations seem to have the use of the mails denied to them-Even the personnel connected with those organizations have been denied the use of the mails. How is it the Post Office Department knows what is in those letters? More than that, if they know what is in those letters it would seem to me rank discrimination against a good Canadian citizen to have his mail disturbed and his mailing privileges stopped, when there must be in Canada from time to time communist propaganda of various kinds circulating, and so far as I am aware the Post Office Department has not stopped the mails going to any of those people. This may be carrying out a general policy that may be quite proper, but it does seem to me that if you are going to make scapegoats of Canadians, there are some of these other people whom I would rather see made scapegoats. I think we ought to have something from the minister about that.

The information we receive comes in the form of complaints from various organizations. In these lottery schemes there are always some of those letters that do find their way to the dead letter office.
Supply-Post Office
Just how it happens, I do not know. They are opened there because they do not show any return address on the envelope. Of course when someone puts a lottery ticket in a letter he usually puts his address on the lottery ticket, and that is how we know where the letter comes from.
Unless a mistake is made in the address, you never catch them?
I would not go that far, because that would be encouraging them.

I shall not be long, but since I have not time to read novels, I enjoy myself by reading reference books and making comparisons. According to the Canadian almanac, I see that there are thirteen Ph.D.'s in the Department of Agriculture. The chief of the tobacco division is a Ph.D. I am wondering why, in the list of post office officials, there are no Ph.D.'s. I wonder if they are Ph.D.'s and are too modest to mention it, or if they do not care about it. I should like to know if there are any Ph.D.'s in the Post Office Department, and I intend to ask a question about that of all the departments. I want to know more about mortarboards.

I should like to take about five minutes of the time of the committee to say a word on these estimates, and in doing so to commend the minister on the excellent report he presented to this committee. The fact that we have an income of over $101 million is a credit to his department, and indicates the progress Canada is making generally. I wish to say a word about the Post Office Department, because I believe it is rather unique amongst the various departments of government in the fact that it serves all the people of Canada. The Department of Agriculture serves the agricultural interests of the country; the Department of Transport serves the great ramifications of the transportation system of our country, and the same is true of other departments, but the postal department is one that is interested in every man, woman, and child in the Dominion of Canada.
As the Postmaster General has indicated, there are 46,000 people employed in this department. I believe every member of this house will agree that those 46,000 employees have done a marvellous job in the capacity in which they are working. I believe every member of the house will also agree that, particularly at the Christmas season, they do a excellent job in dispatching the mails day by day. I should like to add a word to what the member for Peel stated in regard to rural mail administration. The rural mail delivery service is one that we in rural Canada do

Supply-Post Office
appreciate greatly. We accept it as part of the great network of services rendered to the people of rural Canada. It was in the year 1908 that the Postmaster General inaugurated the first rural postal delivery service in Canada, patterned on a plan in effect in the United States. This delivery service has grown rapidly, as the Postmaster General has said, until today it serves almost 350,000 boxholders across this dominion in those great areas that lie outside our towns and cities.
The reason, Mr. Chairman, for this brief outline is to bring to this committee a general picture of how the rural people of Canada depend upon this delivery service. I do feel that the rural mail couriers are perhaps the lowest paid class of people in Canada. I was glad to hear the Postmaster General mention the setting up of a plan for the improvement of the rural mail couriers' situation. I know the member for Temiscouata will not approve, but I do believe a committee should be set up to review this whole situation with a view to improving conditions for the rural mail couriers. The average mail route, particularly in the area from which I come, is twenty-five miles in length. The mail couriers average about four stops per mile, so that means about one hundred stops during the route. I believe that a rate of pay of about nine cents per mile would be a fair allocation of the cost of mail service. For the average twenty-five mile route, the courier would travel 7,500 miles a year. It would cost about $675 to operate a motorcar in the section where I live, and there would be approximately $575 left for his income after his operational costs were paid, basing it on a $50 per mile tender.
I do feel, Mr. Chairman, in view of the foregoing remarks, that the minister should take into consideration the facts I have mentioned. I realize that a great many people will say that tenders were called and were accepted. That is true, and in most cases I suppose the lowest tender was accepted. At the same time, many of those tenders were called for at a time when figures on cost were going down, and instead of that they have increased. The cost of operating motorcars has increased since those tenders were accepted. I believe some consideration should be given to that fact. All over rural Ontario we find that the mail .couriers have to drive older model cars in order to show a profit on the operation. I do say that should not be. The custodian of the king's mail should be able to drive a motorcar that is in keeping with his duties. I know a particular mail courier who has had a route for thirty-three years. He was telling me he had to tender so low in order to get the position that
[Mr. Catherwood.l
he is no further ahead today than he was. when he started. I believe that a committee, as suggested by the hon. member for Peel,, could take all these matters into consideration. After so many years' satisfactory service with the department, I believe these men should come under the superannuation system. I hope the minister will take these matters into consideration.
I shall certainly take them into consideration, but I do not think any members of this service would like to be government employees. If we gave them salaries, they would be.

I should like to take up with the Postmaster General three matters which are of concern: to my constituency, but I think they cover problems which are common to other constituencies as well. The first of these is the question of the extension of the air mail service to two areas where scheduled flights have recently been inaugurated. The first of these is between Kamloops and Penticton. It serves the cities of Kamloops, Vernon, Kelowna and Penticton. The other is the service from Vancouver to Prince George, via Kamloops, Williams Lake and Quesnel. That service goes on to Fort St. John.
This matter has been discussed with the department ever since the services were inaugurated, and I regret to have to say that the decision so far has not been favourable, even though for a time the Acting Postmaster General-that is, the Solicitor General-was looking after the affairs of the department. Although the Postmaster General, whom we are all glad to see back here today, said that the Acting Postmaster General was generous during his absence, I regret to say that his generosity did not extend to approving air mail service on those two routes, as requested. Now that the Postmaster General is back and restored to health, perhaps he will be feeling generous, and I am encouraged to believe that we can hope for success in making this request.
I base the request for air mail service on these routes on two premises: first, the populations to be served, which speak for themselves; and second, the necessity of giving a better service to those areas, and particularly perhaps to the area of the Cariboo, than they have had in the past. I understand that the principle is that air mail service will not be approved where surface mail provides an alternative delivery as fast as it can be delivered by air mail. In this respect the argument that I am about to make applies particularly to the service from Vancouver to Kamloops, Williams Lake

and on up to the north, because those areas up through the Cariboo are not served adequately by daily surface mail.
Here I want to advance again an argument that I have advanced before with respect to the development of our pioneer districts. No one will object, on the face of it, to the inauguration of the all-up air mail service; but that service applies at the moment only to the main line T.C.A. routes between our main centres, and those centres were already served by a good surface mail system. There were no great delays in the delivery of mail between our large cities. While, as I say, no one could object to the general principle of improving and speeding up that system, I feel that the pioneer areas which suffer from an inadequate mail service are entitled to at least as much consideration and are certainly entitled to have their inadequate mail service made adequate when other areas have their adequate service made superlative. The mail services in the districts to which I refer are certainly not first-class.
Another argument in that regard is that those areas pay their full and fair share of taxes; and the inauguration of all-up air mail service on the main lines does not benefit them. They do not begrudge, and speaking as their representative I do not begrudge, the superlative service which all-up air mail service gives; but the point I want to urge strongly is that the tax money of the people in the pioneer areas, in its proportion, goes to support those superlative or improved services whereas they themselves get no corresponding benefit or improvement in service. I think that they are entitled now to have a recognition of their position and, where the facilities make it possible, as is now the case with the institution of these scheduled air services to which I have referred, they are entitled to have their tax contribution recognized by improving their services, and by granting in this case an air mail service on the Vancouver, Kamloops, Williams Lake, Prince George run.
Mr. Murray (Caribool: May I ask a question, Mr. Chairman?
Perhaps the hon. member might address his question to the Postmaster General when I have finished.
I should like to ask a question of the hon. member who is speaking. He is making a statement which is not just factual.

What I would suggest is this, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. gentleman thinks that my plea for the area that I represent is not justified-
Supply-Post Office
I was asking you to stop at the boundary.
Order. The hon. member for Kamloops has the floor.
Let him ask a question.

Incidentally, if what I gather from the interruption of the hon. member for Cariboo is that he does not wish the extension of the air mail service beyond Williams Lake to his constituency, I should be glad indeed to confine the request in the remarks I have made to my own constituency.
With this request for that air mail service, I should like to couple a request for a daily mail service by surface to the way post offices up the Cariboo highway. I have taken this matter up previously with the department, and an investigation was made into the cost. The figures produced were said to be such that the cost of the increased service made it impossible to approve the request. I do not know the basis upon which the department made this investigation and obtained the figures, but I was advised that they were obtained from one carrier only. What I want to suggest to the minister is that he should obtain figures from other carriers who serve the area.
My suggestion is this. The mail might be carried to Williams Lake by the present service from Ashcroft, and the possibility should be investigated of having some of the trucking lines make a distribution from Williams Lake on their journeys up and down the Cariboo highway; or alternately, the possibility should be investigated of having them make a distribution from Ashcroft.
I have a great deal of correspondence on this matter; and a number of my correspondents advise me that over the past twenty years there has been no improvement in the mail service in these areas on the Cariboo highway. Twenty years is a long time to wait for an improvement in the mail service. As a matter of fact, in the old days when they had the horse-drawn stage coaches, those points had a better mail service than they have now, because then they had a daily mail service. Now most of those points have service only three times a week in the summertime, by the P.G.E., and twice a week in the wintertime. To those people who depend on these post offices up and down the Cariboo highway, many of whom are in business, running tourist camps and guest camps, the present system results in a serious loss of business; because by the time a person will write in from, say, Seattle or some other point down in the states, and the letter comes through Vancouver and up the P.G.E., it is not delivered to these points until perhaps four

Supply-Post Office
days after it has been written; then by the time it goes out on the rural mail route and a reply is sent in and back down via the P.G.E. from the post office, it is up to ten days before the writer of the letter receives an answer. I have been told of cases where business has been lost as a consequence, because those writing in for reservations or to find out if they can be accommodated at certain times will not wait that long for a reply. Since there is a daily stage service and trucking service passing directly up and down the Cariboo highway it is time that these people received daily mail service to the way post offices on that route. I again advance the argument that these people contribute their full share of taxes to the general revenue of the country. If we can institute a superservice by way of an all-up air mail to areas which were already receiving a fast surface delivery, surely it is time' that we provided an adequate service to those areas which have been struggling for so long with an inadequate mail delivery.
I appreciate the work that the Post Office Department does. I am sure that the Postmaster General would like to grant these requests, and if he feels that he has not yet been able to justify it, I urge him to bear in mind these considerations on which I have based the request. These people contribute their share of taxes. In proportion they pay just as much as the other areas, and it is not fair to penalize them any longer, and to deny them longer the adequate service to which they are entitled, and which they need.
Then I should like to ask the Postmaster General if he will consider another matter, and here I am speaking also on behalf of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). It is a question involving the shipment of parcels to the United Kingdom. It has been drawn to my attention that many people have found-and I have personal knowledge of this-that food parcels have been lost and no trace can be found of them; and no report can be made of what has happened. This has had a cumulative effect and lias discouraged people from sending parcels. The suggestion has been made that some process be worked out whereby it would be possible to trace the parcel from the time of mailing to the time of delivery or loss. Could such a system be instituted with respect to parcels to the United Kingdom without great expense? I appreciate that if it were very expensive the department would be reluctant to do it. Would a system comparable to the registration system be feasible with respect to these parcels? Even if it were necessary to charge three cents or five cents for the registration, could it be done on that

basis so as to provide a means of tracing the parcel? Will the Postmaster General give us an answer to that question?

The expense of registration
would be about 25 cents per package. That would be half of the actual rate.
I put this before the Postmaster General: the expense of registering a letter is only 10 cents. I wonder whether it would not be possible to-
Registration price and cost are not the same. The price is 10 cents; the cost is 20 cents.

We will never get a perfect mail service. That would be a service where the deliveries would be made every hour or so even if you were out on the Cariboo road or back in the Peace river country. I must take the hon. member for Kamloops to task to a certain extent. Of course he is doing good work when he is urging the department to extend service.
Do you want to go back to the dog team days?

No, nor the horse and buggy days or the stage coach days. The situation on the Cariboo road today

and I speak with direct knowledge of course- is this. At the town of Quesnel we receive at least one air mail service daily, and at the town of Prince George somewhat further on we receive two air mail services daily, plus the rail service, plus the mail that is hauled in by the stage. Below Quesnel we have the rural route recently installed. Coming then further along the Cariboo road we certainly have a very good service, but not throughout its entire length, but certainly in that area. Out of Prince George we have two rural routes, and we are going along very nicely along the Cariboo road. Back in the country for some distance in some of these mining camps, and so on, the deliveries are not as regular as they might be, but you must expect that in a rough country.
While I am commenting here, I join with the hon. member for Kamloops, in asking for a little more money for some of our post offices. We have a very good country up there and the revenues are good, especially at Dawson Creek and at some other points, namely, Fort St. John and Quesnel. All that we need is about $50,000 post offices at each of these points and we would be delightedly happy.
I want to say a word with regard to these couriers. It is unfortunate that these people are encouraged to bid against each other until the mail which is hauled by land up there is often hauled at much less than

the cost of transportation. The department might put a base price on for hauling the mail. Something should be done along that line, and in the meantime I want to thank the minister for the excellent service being given at Quesnel and all through other points in the Cariboo riding.
Will the minister comment on my request for more service?
I have taken due note of the requests and I shall consider them.

I should like to join the hon. member for Cariboo in expressing to the Postmaster General and to his efficient administrative staff my appreciation of the excellent job they have done throughout Canada, and particularly in my own riding, and I am quite sure in all ridings. As far as I am concerned I was particularly pleased to hear the hon. member for Cariboo express his thanks for the service which has been given to the city of Prince George, which is a very fine city. I do not think it is quite in the same class as the Comox-Courtenay area and the Campbell River area. I would like the minister further to consider the proposition I have offered him that we should also receive only one first-class air mail service a day. We have an air passenger service in there twice a day now. We would be quite content to accept just one service by plane a day. I would ask the Postmaster General to see if it is not possible for him to extend that service to that area in the very near future.

There are just one or two small matters that I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General before this item carries. First, a word in connection with the rural directories. I should like to know whether it is possible to have greater co-operation from the postmasters at various country post offices because the directories are not at all up to date. In some instances we get from fifty to sixty or seventy-five letters back that are sent out according to the latest directories.

speechtext:
Since it appears that at least one hon. member wishes to speak on this item, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should make a brief statement. This vote covers moneys required (1) to complete the veterans' housing programs, with $18,500,000 required for that purpose; (2) to complete the 1949-50 program of houses for the use of married personnel in the three armed services, an amount of $26,500,000; (3) to construct the 1949-50 program of schools and services for housing projects built in army camps, air stations and naval establishments, in the amount of $10 million; and (4) to finance the 1950 program for houses for married personnel of the Department of National Defence as well as ground services for such houses, an amount of $20 million.
The 1949 veterans' rental program amounted in all to 4,798 units. As at March 31, 1950, there were 1,415 units still to be started, as well as 2,278 units which had been started before March 31, 1950, but which were still to be completed. This, together with some landscaping and miscellaneous work to complete the 1948 program, involves $18,500,000.
The sum of $26,500, is required to complete houses for married service personnel. The 1949 program amounted to 4,530 units in thirty-four projects. As at the end of the fiscal year 273 of these units were completed and 2,585 had been started but were not complete. Some 1,672 units were to be started after March 31, 1950.
Arrangements have been made under which approximately $10 million is required for twenty-two schools. In every province we received co-operation from the department of education, both in respect to the design and type of school as well as to its operation after completion.
Though the 1950 program for married personnel for the Department of National Defence is still under consideration, we have included in this estimate an amount of $20 million to provide for approximately 2,000 additional houses. Because basic arrangements have been determined with the Department of National Defence for the 1949 program, it is anticipated that an earlier start can be made this year than last. I hope that all contracts will be awarded for the 1950 program, with very few exceptions, before too long.
Hon. members will recall that though this construction is carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation each project, both in respect to the number of units and their cost, is approved by treasury board
Mr. Speaker.]

before Central Mortgage undertakes the contract. The government has not finally determined the size of the 1950 housing program for the Department of National Defence, but should it exceed 2,000 units additional funds will be requested at a later date.
During the first four months of 1950 residential construction has continued at approximately the same level as during 1949. During the first quarter of 1950 new residential starts in all parts of the country were 5 [DOT] 5 per cent above those in the corresponding period of 1949. Completions during the first quarter of 1950 were almost the same as in the first quarter of 1949. In cities and towns with populations of 5,000 and over, starts during the first four months of 1950 were 12-2 per cent in excess of starts in the same period in 1949. This reflects greater residential activity in the maritimes, Quebec and Ontario. Starts in the prairies and British Columbia were three per cent and ten per cent respectively below starts in the first four months of last year.
I wish to emphasize, however, that because of climatic and other conditions, starts during the first three or four months of any year may or may not be indicative of a trend for the year as a whole. It will be recalled that although first quarter starts in 1949 exceeded those for 1948, 1949 starts for the year as a whole were slightly below those of 1948.
Furthermore, the recent change in the lumber situation may have an important bearing upon the number of starts in 1949. Prices of lumber have increased sharply in all parts of the country, and there is now evidence that even at increased prices lumber is not readily available to house builders. In the program of married quarters for the Department of National Defence, four projects have been postponed because the prices bid by contractors range from $800 to $1,300 per unit above prices for similar houses in 1949. We do not intend to proceed with projects at this price level.
The same trend is showing in private house building. The cost of individual houses will increase, and already in certain areas there is a shortage of lumber which is stopping the framing of houses. This condition is likely to reduce the number of new starts for the year, notwithstanding an increase in the number of new starts during the first four months of 1950.
The increase in price is occasioned by the buoyant demand for lumber in the United States. This has had the effect of a sharp increase in prices in the United States, with the result that our exports to that country have increased to such a point that domestic supply is not generally sufficient.

As far as the operations of central mortgage are concerned, we have no intention of supporting the "demand" side of the market by building married quarters at greatly increased prices, nor do we intend to adjust loans under the National Housing Act to take care of marked increases in cost both to the builder and the home owner resulting from the increase in the price of lumber. We deem it better to face a decline in the number of starts rather than add to the inflationary trend. For these reasons I cannot give the house an estimate of starts and completions for the year 1950.
Hon. members will recall that the National Housing Act was amended at the last session of parliament by the introduction-through section 35-of an arrangement for the federal government and the provinces to enter into agreements which would lead to public assistance in the field of housing. When the various provincial legislatures met this spring, seven of the ten provinces passed legislation complementary to section 35 of the National Housing Act. Since then we have been working with the provinces to determine mutually satisfactory activity in this field. Activity in some twenty to thirty municipalities has now been discussed with the provincial governments. Over-all agreements with Ontario and British Columbia have been entered into whereby preliminary expenses may be incurred.
In Ontario there is a lack of serviced land within the larger municipalities. At this stage we are working with the Ontario government towards a substantial number of land assembly projects, whereby land will be serviced and made available to private builders who are prepared to build houses of a type and at a price satisfactory to the two governments.
The province of New Brunswick is actively considering proposals for housing in the city of Saint John. Today we received a proposal from the government for a housing project in that city.
Because of flood conditions it is not likely that a start will be made in the use of this legislation in Manitoba in 1950. Preliminary conversations were under way with the Manitoba government, but have been suspended during the period of emergency in that province.
In British Columbia negotiations are under way, and I hope that before long it will be possible to announce the projects which will be undertaken in that province.
Preliminary conversations have taken place with Saskatchewan, although we have not yet reached a point where specific projects are under consideration.
Supply-Resources and Development
An agreement has been signed with the government of Newfoundland for a subsidized low rental housing project in the city of St. John's involving 140 units. The contract has been awarded and construction has started. Negotiations are under way with the government of Newfoundland for the installation of services such as water, sewer, roads and sidewalks for a land assembly project of approximately 100 acres. The purpose is to make serviced lots available to individuals who wish to build homes.
Changes made in the National Housing Act at the last session have doubtless been an important factor in the increase in the number of joint loans. Some 8,800 units have been approved under part I of the act during the first four months of 1950, as compared with 4,650 units in the same period in 1949 

an increase of almost 90 per cent.
