speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is rather remarkable that this is the first occasion in this 1950 session when there has been a debate on the subject of housing. It is no doubt regrettable, but it seems that this is the first occasion, in the absence of any legislation dealing with housing, for any extended discussion on the situation. I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, even under those circumstances to speak at length. We are so close to the end of the session, it seems to me that the occasion calls only for touching on the highlights of the situation, rather than for an extended review of the problem. I do hope, however, that the fact that the debate on this occasion may be brief, and the fact that there was little said about housing at this session, will not be construed by anyone as indicating, on the part of the house, a feeling that the housing problem has greatly improved.
One wishes that at this late date, June, 1950, one could say that the housing problem has shown substantial improvement. But one cannot say that. The problem is still very serious, and has grave aspects to it. The minister has touched on certain figures in regard to completions and starts. The figures that were released on June 16 by the dominion bureau of statistics indicate that in the first quarter of 1950 completions totalled 17,873 as compared with 17,826 in the first quarter of 1949. The results of completions thus are almost the same. Starts in the first quarter of 1950 numbered 9,015, as compared with 8,396 in 1949. At the end of March there were 50,161 units under construction as compared with 46,886 a year earlier.
4222	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development
The same bulletin issued by the dominion bureau of statistics, Mr. Chairman, has this interesting comment to add:
From the types of dwelling units constructed during the first quarter of 1950, it is estimated that 28 per cent were for rental purposes, showing no change from the same period of 1949.
So that relatively, of the housing that is now becoming available, the proportion available for rental purposes, of which the need is very acute, has not increased.
Members who sat in the last parliament have been accustomed to hearing the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he had Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in his department, touch upon the question of the relationship between the housing problem and the family formation rate. How he used to let that expression, "the family formation rate", with its alliteration, roll off the end of his tongue! On June 23 the dominion bureau of statistics issued some figures as a result of a study in that field. The bulletin reads as follows:
Between June, 1941, and June, 1949, the number of families in Canada increased by slightly more than 26 per cent and the number of households by slightly more than 24 per cent, according to estimates by the dominion bureau of statistics. Since 1947, however, the rise in number of households has exceeded the increase in number of families.
The estimated number of households in June, 1949, was 3,360,000, an increase of 125,000 or 3-9 per cent over the estimated 3,235,000 in June, 1948, and
232.000	or 7-4 per cent over the estimated 3,128,000 in June, 1947. In comparison, the estimated number of families was 3,187,000 in June last year, showing a rise of 99,000 or 3-2 per cent over the estimated
3.088.000	a year earlier and 150,000 or just under five per cent over the total of 3,037,000 in June, 1947.
Now, sir, it may be that those figures, in the light of the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in earlier sessions, are capable of having more than one inference drawn from them. I think, however, that this is at least one inference that may be drawn from these figures: if we are not making the progress with the housing problem that we should like to see made, it can no longer be attributable to any acceleration of the family formation rate over the rate at which housing is being constructed.
Building costs today are a serious problem in relation to the construction of housing accommodation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said on June 23 that "building costs have risen substantially since last September." That is an unfortunate fact, particularly with respect to certain classes of building materials. I place that statement alongside a statement appearing in the January quarterly issue of "Housing in Canada",


the publication of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in which we find on page 23 this statement:
The trend in house-building costs showed a distinct tendency to level off in 1949.
That seemed to be the picture that confronted the house when the housing question was last discussed in this chamber at the end of November, seven months ago; and I think many members of the house indulged in some hopefulness on the subject, feeling that now, with a measure of stability in housing costs appearing, more people would find it within their means to build. But the fact that housing construction costs seem to be rising again does give cause for concern when we measure the still tremendous shortage of housing in Canada. The need of rental housing is still acute. Many of the purchases of new houses that are being made today are being made by people who are stretching every resource to buy or to build because rental accommodation is not available to them, or is not available to them at a rental that they can afford to pay. One views that fact with some degree of deep concern, because if we should encounter anything in the way of a recession in this country-and we hope that will not occur-and if land and building values should fall, it may leave many of these people, particularly the young people among them, with grave problems on their hands in financing these purchases on which they have embarked.
Marginal purchasers have been coming into the house purchasing market to a greater extent than previously. I do not mean to say that there are more purchasers in the market but I do say that, of those who are purchasing today, a much higher percentage falls within the class of marginal purchasers than ever before. We hope that the wage and salary levels in this country will be maintained so that those people will not be faced with a serious problem in meeting their obligations under their purchases.
The supply of building materials still presents some serious difficulties. Steel has been coming off control this year and we are told in the booklet "Supply of Building Materials in Canada: "Outlook, 1950", issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, that most steel supplies, as they enter into house construction, are going to be available in greater quantities than previously. However, our familiar subject of nails is one that is still cause for some concern. On page 11 of this issue we read1:
Imports of finished nails have been heavy, increasing from 6,300 tons in 1948 to 13,300 tons in 1949. Canadian mills have also proceeded to manufacture nails at a higher rate.

Then this disquieting sentence appears at the conclusion of the paragraph:
However, wire nails and certain gauges of steel sheet and small sizes of pipe were still difficult to obtain in necessary quantities.
There are also some other kinds of building materials that are admittedly not in too plentiful supply. But the most serious problem confronting those engaged in house construction today, from the point of view of the supply of building materials, relates to lumber. As often happens, the scarcity of a commodity may not be general in all parts of the country; but certainly in the part of the country from which I come the scarcity of lumber is presenting serious problems. At page 6 of this booklet we read the following paragraph:
The domestic supply of lumber Is not expected to change materially in 1950-
And I interject here, Mr. Chairman, that this pamphlet was issued in February last. -and special types and grades may still be difficult to procure despite the fact that production may at least equal 1949 levels. Sales in the United States are expected to continue at a relatively high level throughout the year and any possible decrease in United Kingdom contracts may be taken up by that market. Besides this, manufacturers' inventories are at a low level and United States prices are appreciably above those in Canada. Therefore, it appears that prime quality lumber suitable for sale abroad may not be readily available in Canada throughout 1950. Export controls on lumber and wood building materials with the exception of pulp and fibre wallboard were discontinued at the end of last year.
The problem of lumber supply is assuming quite serious proportions in view of the way in which the market in the United States has been draining off some of the most suitable lumber in Canada for building purposes.
Mr. Chairman, let me now turn briefly to the subject of legislation. The amendments to the National Housing Act which were enacted by parliament at the end of November, 1949, came too late in that year to make much impression as yet. It had been hoped that, with the opening of the building season in earnest this spring, agreements might have been entered into which would provide for extensive use of the provisions of the new section 35 of the act. There have been difficulties in the way-the minister has referred to some of them- such as the necessity of negotiation with the provinces and the difficulties confronting many of the municipalities with whom, after all, these projects must be initiated. As one may fairly repeat on looking back, I think it is regrettable that those amendments were not introduced at a much earlier date. As to the municipalities, this committee must
Supply-Resources and Development recognize the fact that the municipalities- particularly those that are faced with the most acute housing	problems-have	a
variety of complex problems on their hands. The minister has referred to the shortage of serviced land. That situation is particularly serious in some of the larger urban municipalities and their suburban areas. For instance, in the city of Toronto-that is, metropolitan Toronto, greater Toronto-this is an extremely serious problem. It also has a relation to the other financial problems that these municipalities are facing, because many of the municipalities, particularly the suburban municipalities surrounding the large cities, are themselves faced with so many problems that the provision of serviced land itself offers to them in many cases problems with which they are not financially able to cope.
One welcomes the evidence that a number of the provinces have entered into agreement, and are prepared in this way to pave the way for the use of the provisions of section 35 of the act for the benefit of projects in certain of their municipalities.
I cannot forbear, sir, Irom expressing the hope, as I did when these amendments were under discussion in the house last November, that steps will be taken to broaden the provisions of section 12 of the act, so that it may not be more difficult for municipalities to proceed with redevelopment projects in crowded areas and slum areas than to proceed with development projects that do not involve the clearing of areas that have been built up in the municipality. You will remember, sir, that under section 35 the dominion contributes 75 per cent of the cost and bears 75 per cent of loss; whereas the province is called upon to bear only 25 per cent. But in the case of slum clearance projects or redevelopment projects, which are seriously needed in many of the urban areas, the provisions of section 12 remain, and the municipality must find 50 per cent of the cost of acquiring and clearing the land. I submit to the minister that the government must recognize the social and economic aspects of this problem, and that there is no justification for this discrimination between new development and redevelopment projects.
Sir, there is one final matter upon which I think the committee will wish to ask the minister for more information. As I followed his remarks none was given by the minister on this subject in his introductory statement. I am asking about the extent to which the new amendments to section 4 of the act in relation to second mortgages have been put to use.

Supply-Resources and Development
The minister did not give a very encouraging picture in regard to the mortgage lending operations under the National Housing Act. In fact he has said that, faced with rising building costs again this year, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not prepared to raise its lending values. One can sympathize with the corporation in this problem; one can frankly say that one does not wish to see the corporation participating in a process which may be inflationary in its nature; nevertheless, sir, unless the department presided over by the minister is prepared to say that this present rise in building costs is only very temporary, then I am afraid the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is going to have to face the facts. They will have to make up their minds whether this rise in building costs is to be shortlived, or whether it threatens to be of long duration; because, if it is of long duration, then I submit, sir, that the provisions of this act will be at least in part nullified by freezing the lending values of houses to be constructed under the terms of this act.
We had this problem in previous sessions and some of us had to complain strenuously that many of the beneficial provisions of the National Housing Act were denied that beneficial operation which parliament intended when it enacted those provisions, by such an administration of those provisions as has largely nullified their operation by insisting on writing down lending value. I have admitted that the problem is not free from difficulty. I see the difficulties facing the administration in this respect, but, sir, unless they are prepared to say that this present rise in building costs is to be very short-lived, then I am afraid they will simply have to accept the situation and raise lending values in keeping with the rise in building costs.
In that' regard one may well ask, Mr. Chairman, as to what use has been made in the meantime of the amendments to section 4 of the act. The committee will recall that new subsection 3 was added to that section of the act last November, in these words:
In addition to the joint loan referred to in this section a loan may be made by the corporation to the home owner or home purchaser in an amount not exceeding one-sixth of the joint loan if the cost of the house to the home owner or the purchase price thereof to the home purchaser is, in the opinion of the corporation, fair and reasonable.
You remember, sir, this was pictured to us as the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation going into the second mortgage field to supply a need that was represented in the widening split between the cost of house construction or house purchase on the one hand and the amount available by way of first mortgage under the National Housing Act up to the lending

value on the other hand. When this measure was under consideration some of us pointed out that while it purported to fill the gap and while the province of Ontario, for instance, which had entered this field nearly two years before, was in the face of this legislation now withdrawing from that field as there would be no further need for them to be in it, the efficacy of this section would depend very largely upon the interpretation and administration of it. Therefore I ask the minister whether he will give the committee some report on the operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under that section, and in doing so I express the hope that that new provision to which great hope was attached in all quarters of the house-certainly much was made of it by the government in introducing the amendment-has not been nullified by rigidity in the administration of the act and of the section by those charged with administration in the department and in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; because if lending value is to be frozen, and rigid interpretation is to be given to the provisions of this section and of the sections in relation to lending value applied to the old first mortgage then, Mr. Chairman, the house might as well have spared itself some of the efforts put into amending this act in 1949.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, whether one agrees with the hon. member for Eglinton or not, it is evident that tonight he has offered some constructive remarks. He said there was no debate on housing at this session, and that no new housing legislation has been passed. I wonder seriously if he needs new legislation to get elevated inspiration for a fine speech?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with many of the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Eglinton, and I shall not take the time of the committee to repeat those things with which I agree. There are however some aspects of the problem of housing which I suggest might well be underlined both from my own point of view and from that of the people in constituencies such as the one I have the honour to represent.
We have heard tonight, as we always hear when this subject comes up, a number of statistics. We have heard references to the legislation on the statute books. But the fact remains that despite statistics, despite legislation, despite the large number of very fine homes in Canada-and I, for one, am very happy to see more and more fine homes across this land-despite all those things, the fact remains that for thousands of our people

fine homes, even decent homes in which to live, are still dreams of the distant future.
Constituencies such as the one I represent have in them thousands of people who live in overcrowded conditions in the kind of housing that certainly does no credit to twentieth century civilization. I plead again for more of a social conscience in connection with this question, for greater realization on the part of the government that it is our collective responsibility as a people to do what we can to solve this social problem, and to see to it that all our people have a chance to live in decent homes.
To bring that down to some of the specific things that should be done, I should like to say a word about the matter of low-rental housing. I realize, as does the hon. member for Eglinton, that section 35 was written into the National Housing Act last fall to make provision for low-rental projects on a 75/25 basis. That basis involves the province putting up 25 per cent of the cost of such a project, the dominion putting up 75 per cent, and the two jurisdictions taking any loss that might follow in those proportions.
However, despite the fact that that legislation is there, provinces such as the one I come from have not seen fit to take advantage of it; and it has been represented to me that although some of the provinces feel that they might be able to stand 25 per cent of the loss involved in a low-rental housing project, they could not stand the financing of 25 per cent of the capital cost. I still hope that some projects under that plan will get going. Certainly there is pressure being exerted at all levels of government and by all groups of people in my province, and particularly in my city, to have the government of Manitoba enter this field. However, I think it becomes obvious already, even though the minister may say that we should give section 35 of the act more than six or seven months' trial, that it is not going to be the beginning of a great program of low-rental housing for the people of this country who need it.
I insist that when we talk about low-rental housing, particularly for the working people in industrial areas, it should be not just the kind of buildings that provide roofs over the heads of families, but rather it should be a modern layout that makes available to our workers and their families the best that modern architects, engineers and community planners can design for modern healthful and decent living.
I am one of those who last November welcomed the step taken in this legislation, but I submit that in the face of the problem, and in the face of the challenge that presents
Supply-Resources and Development itself to us as a civilized nation to do something in the field of housing, we have not even started.
In addition to this problem of more effective legislation in the matter of low-rental housing, it must also be pointed out, as has been done by the hon. member for Eglinton, that there is room for real improvement by way of redevelopment or slum clearance under section 12 of the act. There again the minister can say that the legislation is on the statute books-indeed, it has been on the statute books considerably longer than has section 35; indeed it has been there for the last six years. However, the amount of slum clearance and redevelopment of housing areas that has taken place under that legislation certainly is nothing to write home about.
Then, may I refer to the rising cost of building that has taken place particularly since export controls were taken off and Canadian lumber allowed to go freely to the higher priced market in the United States. The result has been that prices for lumber are rising in this country, too. I heard a news report over the radio, or saw it in the press not long ago, to the effect that it was hoped that these increased lumber prices would not result in a rise of more than two or three per cent in building costs. But when one thinks of two or three per cent in terms of $10,000 or $12,000, or whatever it costs to build a house today, he realizes it is quite a sum.
Somehow or other these percentage increases seem to have a way of pyramiding and making it more difficult for people to get decent homes. So whether it is in the field of low-rental housing for people who cannot afford to have their own homes, or in the field of home ownership, which is certainly desirable, the barriers which crop up seem to wipe out, almost before they are enjoyed, any of the advantages found in the legislation the government brings down from time to time.
I should like to ask the minister a question regarding the quality of lumber and building materials and also the inspection service that is available. It -has been represented to me that the urgency of the situation and the need people have to get lumber are such that there are cases of second-grade lumber being sold as first-grade, or at first-grade prices, thus adding to the cost of building and reducing the quality.
Surely our people deserve protection in this field. I would ask the minister whether Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are interesting themselves in this phase of the matter. I do not need to take more time
4226	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development to emphasize the importance of the problem. It is unfortunate that the layout of the session is such that we have not reached this important problem until what may be the next to the last day. I do urge however that hon. members in all quarters of the house, and the government in particular, look upon this question of housing not just as a case of putting a roof over the head of every Canadian, but rather as a real challenge to use all the ingenuity we possess and all the advances that have been made in architecture, engineering and community planning really to house our Canadian people at the standard they deserve.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with what has been said by the two previous speakers I agree, and I believe every other member of the house will also agree. Nevertheless that does not come anywhere near finding a solution to the problem, something which we all desire. The simple facts confronting us at the present time are that the cost of building a house, such as the great majority of the Canadian people deserve to have, is so high that they simply cannot afford it. The taxes on such a property will be so high that the income of the average Canadian will not be sufficient to enable him to pay such an amount. The cost will be so high that the Canadian of average income will be unable to pay for his home, so that whichever way he looks at it he stands to have a number of years of headaches and worry, and then lose his home.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
There are three or four Liberals who I hope will speak later on and have something more than "carried" to say in their speeches. What are we going to do about the problem? Has the minister given any thought to the possibility of purchasing prefabricated houses from Great Britain? It seems to me that not so long ago I read that Australia had made an agreement with Great Britain for a certain number of prefabricated houses to be delivered at a price far lower than it was possible for Australia to build comparable houses. It seems to me I heard that New Zealand had made a similar bargain with Great Britain. Has the minister given any thought to making an arrangement with Great Britain for prefabricated houses?
I should also like the minister to give the house some account of what he has been able to discover in his studies as to the possibility of using aluminum for prefabrication in Canada. Certainly we do not have to go without houses in this country because the lumbermen choose to run the price of lumber up so high that they render building economically impracticable. Can the minister tell us what he has found with respect to aluminum?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
I do not know whether hon. members will wish me to assume that everybody has spoken and that I should deal with the questions they have raised now. The hon. member for Eglinton requested some information as to the effectiveness of the one-sixth additional loan provided under the act last year. As he said, it replaces the second mortgage that Ontario was making available. I think it can be said that the position the federal government has taken, which has enabled Ontario to withdraw from their second mortgage arrangement, has been entirely satisfactory to the government of Ontario, and I put that forth as evidence of-the fact that it has worked.
As I pointed out when introducing these estimates, some 8,800 units have been approved under part I of the act during the first four months of 1950 compared with 4,650 units in the same period of 1949, an increase of almost 90 per cent. I think it fair to say that can be attributed largely to the additional amount of loan made available by the revision of the act last year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: May I ask the minister if the additional one-sixth was made available in the case of each of the 8,800?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The additional one-sixth is made available for about 75 per cent of all houses that are qualifying for loans under the N.H.A. joint loan arrangements.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: That is about 6,600 of the 8,800.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: And what was the figure for the previous year?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: There were 4,650 units in the same period of the previous year. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre deplored the fact there was not sufficient development of low-cost subsidized housing. I say again, as I said last year, that the revision of the act, as enacted by parliament last year, is broad enough to enter that field of housing, as in fact we have done in Newfoundland, and are prepared to do in any other province that wishes to participate. The hon. member spoke about slum clearance. We realize that there are shortcomings in the application of the slum clearance section. It has not been as broadly applied as one might expect that it would be. If the hon. member will refer to page 7 of the annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for 1949 he will see set out there, in what I consider to be a logical way, the reasons why the slum clearance section has not found broader application to date.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Will the minister say whether the government will reconsider the position it took last November with regard to amending section 12 to bring it into line with the percentages in section 35 in order to assist in redevelopment and slum clearance projects?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The section is under constant consideration. While I cannot of course give the committee any assurance that there will be amendments, I can say that it will be considered, as my hon. friend requests. The hon. member for Lethbridge asked about the use of aluminum. Aluminum has been used by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for siding, insulation, window frames and other incidental parts of houses. It has been used with satisfaction in most regions of Canada but there are some areas where, when aluminum is exposed to the air, it does not stand up too well. The seacoast is one of those areas, and aluminum has been used under those circumstances with only mediocre success.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Can the minister tell us whether he has been in contact with Great Britain to see whether or not the British can supply houses at a price lower than we are able to construct them in Canada?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: We have not been in direct contact with England on that question. There is no evidence at hand to lead us to believe that they can supply houses cheaper than we can. In fact the fabrication of the house is not always the main problem in housing. As my hon. friend knows, the big problem in most instances is the provision of serviced land.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Reverting to the remark made by the minister a short time ago concerning the work done by his department in Newfoundland, I should like to refer to one of those associated with him of whose ability we have a high opinion and for whose interest in Newfoundland we are very grateful. I refer to the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He was in the newest province quite recently. I believe he has concluded certain contracts and made certain arrangements for housing. Will the minister tell us exactly what has happened, and what Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation proposes to do in the future so far as the provision of houses is concerned?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
As I said in general terms, we have entered into an agreement with the province of Newfoundland under section 35 of the act to provide 140 housing units. The basis of participation is 75 per cent by the 55946-267
Supply-Resources and Development federal government and 25 per cent by the government of Newfoundland. The undertaking is that the capital cost will be shared on that basis, and any operating losses that may accrue will also be shared on the same basis. The accommodation is being provided for people in the low income groups, and might be referred to as low rental housing. We have also entered into negotiations with Newfoundland for the servicing of one hundred acres-that is, the provision of water, sewers and all the other elements that go into servicing land-in the city of St. John's. Those are the only two projects that have been worked so far, but we are open to consider any proposals they may lay before us.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Exactly what does servicing mean? Does it mean only providing water and sewers, or also putting up the houses?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
The project I refer to, in
connection with the servicing of one hundred acres, does not include the building of the houses. It has to do with the provision of services normally supplied by a municipality. It is understood that there are builders in Newfoundland who would be prepared to go ahead on a private enterprise basis and construct houses on the land made available by these services.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Is that part of the area known as the St. John's housing corporation area?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I find one remark by the minister very difficult to comprehend. He says the main difficulty is in getting serviced land. That does not make sense to me. I can understand how he might have difficulty getting serviced land in a city like Ottawa, but there are thousands of small towns of 1,500, 2,000 or 2,500 throughout this country that could supply so much serviced land that I do not believe the minister could find enough material in Canada to build the houses; and these towns would be delighted to have more people come there. What is the minister doing about that? Taking my own district, we have towns like Raymond, Picture Butte and Stirling, all in my constituency. There would be no trouble getting serviced lancl there. In view of what I have just brought to his attention, then, how does the statement by the minister make any sense?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
I am differentiating, of
course, between land and serviced land. As everyone knows, plenty of land is available in Canada; but land with the services provided, water, sewers, sidewalks and the like, is not available in the amount required for building houses.
4228	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Still the minister's remarks seem palpably unrealistic to me. The people who lived in this country one hundred and fifty years ago did hot have any of the things he is talking about, yet they carried on, raised their families and made the Canada we have today. Surely it is not necessary to have all these services before we can build houses to shelter the young Canadians who are growing up in our country today. What is the matter with houses in Raymond, Picture Butte and all these other little towns all over Canada; and why cannot houses be built there? Can the minister explain that? For the first forty years of my life I lived without a sidewalk, and I imagine my sons and daughters can do the same. Does the minister not build houses in any places where there are not sidewalks, sewers, water and all the rest of it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. I realize that many houses are going up on land which is not serviced, and that many fine people will grow up in those houses, just as my hon. friend grew up in one. But in this matter of housing we are dealing with municipalities, and, by and large, have to meet their wishes. If they say they do not want houses to go up on land that is not fully serviced, under normal circumstances it is not within our power to proceed. We have to conform to the wishes of the municipalities.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: What is the arrangement with respect to the servicing of this one hundred acres, as far as cost is concerned?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I thought I had outlined that, but perhaps I did not make it clear. The cost of servicing the land-that is, acquiring, assembling and servicing-will be on the 75 per cent 25 per cent participation basis. If the land is then built upon by private contractors the cost of servicing the land will become a charge against the houses then built.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Since the development referred to by the minister is in the constituency I have the honour to represent, I should like to thank him for the interest he has shown in it. It is going to be a great blessing to the people who will be moved from the slum areas *to this new development. It is a good beginning, and I am sure the houses will be more than welcome. Through the kindness of the minister I saw the plan, and I noticed that a playground is to be provided, which will be a great benefit. I am only sorry it was not possible to have more land attached to the houses, and I hope that when another development of this kind is being considered it will be in an area where more land will be

available. This is a good beginning, and I know the people of St. John's are very grateful.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Is this the item under which normally the minister would expect to answer inquiries concerning the sale of wartime houses generally?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Yes, under this item we would consider those questions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I want to ask just this general question, which may only call for a general answer. What is the policy of the department relative to the sale of wartime houses to the tenants now occupying them, particularly in various parts of Ontario?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Generally speaking the policy is that houses built during 1947 and prior to that are being made available to veterans on a sale basis.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: To veterans?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Generally they are the
tenants.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: How large must a community be before it is eligible to have houses built in it? Will the minister build houses in a hamlet or village, or must a community have a population of 1,500, for example? I am still troubled about all those services.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The only requirements we have specified is mutual acceptability as between the federal and provincial governments. If a provincial government were to say it was satisfied to have houses built in a municipality, no matter how small, and asked us to proceed, the chances are that if the project were mutually satisfactory we would do so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
With respect to houses the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has for rent to veterans, has any consideration been given to enlarging the government's policy in order to make those houses available to veterans of world war I, at least in certain cases? I ask this question on the basis of the experience of a world war I veteran in Vancouver, who says that in the area where he wishes to rent a house- he is being put out of his place and therefore needs something else right away- Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have houses vacant but refuse to rent or sell them to veterans of world war I. This case was placed in the hands of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who is now in Geneva. He took it up with Mr. Mansur, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and of course the only answer Mr. Mansur was able to give was that the government had laid it down as a policy that


these houses were to be restricted to veterans of world war II. I understand the reasons for that, but I am wondering if consideration has been given to modifying the policy so as to include veterans of world war I, particularly if, as this correspondent says, there are vacant houses in the district in question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the policy of the government, as approved by this parliament, is to make the houses available only to veterans of world war II.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Is that in any statute?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: No, it is through the vote that parliament makes of funds available for building the houses for veterans of world war II.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I will have to be shown that there has been any decision made by parliament to limit wartime housing to veterans of world war II. Even Mr. Mansur does not blame it on parliament. He says it is a policy laid down by the goyernment. I believe that if the minister will consult with the Minister of Trade and Commerce he will find that this was laid down by government regulation. I hope that matter might be reconsidered.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I think it has been clearly understood by this house, ever since the housing was being considered following world war II, that these houses were being built for the veterans of world war II.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I have listened with a great deal of disappointment to the answers the minister has given. No doubt those are the best answers he can give, Mr. Chairman, but the people of Canada want houses. They do not want to wait 20 years to get them. I say that up to the present time the minister, in explaining the difficulties with which he is confronted, indicates that he will never catch up with the need for houses if he has a thousand years to do it. He had better sit down and plan a real housing program under which the Canadian people will have a real chance to have houses.
Item agreed to.

speechtext: The amount of $300,000 here for emergency shelter is made up as follows: administration expenses, $3,000; projects operated by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, $97,000; municipal and university projects, settlement of leases, restoration of leased land, $100,000; payments re commitments on account of structural maintenance, $100,000. maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
In 1945 the administration of the emergency shelter regulations was a responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board. The principal functions of the administration were to expedite the release of government buildings suitable for conversion to emergency shelter and the bringing of vacant houses into occupancy. By order in council P.C. 7502, of December 28, 1945, the administration was transferred to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As the housing situation became more acute in early 1946, a more positive approach was adopted in emergency shelter matters. Municipalities were directly encouraged to anticipate their shelter needs and to establish a "cushion" of shelter against future demands. To this end the administration began to give financial

assistance to municipalities in connection with "out-of-pocket" expenses of providing emergency shelter. A program was initiated to assist universities to provide emergency shelter for married veteran students and financial aid was granted to universities to cover the cost of providing such accommodation. The pattern of financial assistance was generally grants of one-half the cost-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
