maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I have a question or two to ask the minister, but I am not going to delay the committee as this item was fairly well discussed the other night. There may be some other members, however, who want further information. I want to be brought up to date. I want to know if there is any further communication with the province of Nova Scotia and whether that province has entered into the agreement with respect to the construction of the trans-Canada highway. I should also like to know what proportion of this $20 million that is being provided this year by the federal parliament for the construction of the trans-Canada highway is being earmarked and set aside for the province of Nova Scotia, assuming that an agreement will be entered into. The province of Nova Scotia has announced the location of the trans-Canada highway although we may not all agree with the decision. I said the other night that the Nova Scotia legislature had passed legislation giving authority to build this highway and it would appear that the difficulty with regard to their not entering into the agreement and not having the work proceeded with must be the fault of the minister or of the federal government pending the production by him of the correspondence between himself and Nova Scotia. I should like an answer from the minister before this item passes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: On the question of allocating funds for the province of Nova Scotia, I may say that there has been no attempt to allocate funds for any particular province. We have agreed to undertake to pay for work as it is completed. As I said earlier, we will pay for back work as new work is completed. My hon. friend asked the other night if I would table the correspondence we have had with the province of Nova Scotia. I undertook at that time to contact the government of Nova Scotia. I have done that, but I have not yet heard from them as to whether or not they have changed the stand they took when I put the same question to them previously.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I have just one question. Are you going to have a special trans-Canada highway marker? The reason I ask that question is that in the United States there are such markers on trans-continental roads and I wonder if we are going to have them here, because they are helpful.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
During our conferences we have said that we would leave to the provinces matters of that nature but that if we could help out in any way by co-ordinating the efforts of the provinces, we should be glad to do it. We also expressed the view

Supply-Resources and Development that the Goods Roads Association would also be pleased to have uniformity with respect to such matters.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if the federal government or his department intends to build any of this road themselves, or is it all being built by the different provinces?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The only part of the highway that the federal government itself will build is the highway through national parks.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
I want to bring to the attention of the minister the road that has been proposed through Manitoba, Saskatchewan and up through Alberta. When you consider that, I think you will realize that the point where this highway is going is away from the populated area of the three western provinces. I should like to bring to his attention the fact that from Winnipeg west we have a railroad that belongs to us, to the people of Canada. The highway that is to go through the three provinces in western Canada is to go down along the southern route, which does not help our own railroad. The highway should really and truly head in a northwesterly direction from Winnipeg. It should start out from the bridge at Lock-port and head west till it hits the C.N.R. railroad. It should then hit northwest right through Dauphin and Kamsack. If the road were built that way it would help in another direction during the course of its construction. It would help with regard to the railroad bridges. There are railroad bridges that will have to be built very soon along the Canadian National railroad. They could be put in and serve a double purpose. There is the one across the Assiniboine between Dauphin and Kamsack. There is another one between Humboldt and Saskatoon at Clark's crossing. The highway should follow the Canadian National railroad right from Dauphin. It should run in a northwesterly direction right clean through to Edmonton.
One of the important sections of the agreement was that the road had to go by the shortest route. The route that the highway is taking from Winnipeg west is not the shortest route. It is wrong for the government to spend that large amount of money going down through that dried out area, through a part of the three western provinces where it will not serve the population that it would serve if it were three hundred miles farther north.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Look at the kind of government you have.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
So far as governments are concerned, we have three different kinds in


western Canada. I am not going to say what I think with regard to the payment being made on highways that are not and never will be up to the standard that we expect in western Canada and in all of Canada for a $300 million expenditure.
This money should be expended to give the best service to everybody in Canada. The southern route is not the best route, and it is not the route that will serve the people of Canada best. The southern route goes within fifty miles of No. 2 highway in the United States. That is not rendering a right and proper service to the people of Canada. The development of Canada today, and more especially in western Canada, is in the northern areas. The northern area is the area that will be developed. If anything should be done, then this highway should be headed in a northwestern direction from the big city of Winnipeg to the city that is going to be one of the biggest cities in Canada, namely, Edmonton.
Let me say something else. We should have put the pipe line down alongside the railway. The three should run together, the railway, the highway and the pipe line. Why should they run together? For the simple reason that the people of Canada have a railroad that is running up deficits, and it would help to pay the deficit.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Why did you vote against us?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
The taxes that the people are going to have to pay because of the deficit of the Canadian National Railways could be very easily taken care of by a good highway alongside the people's railroad. The people's railroad is the Canadian National railroad. Where this highway is going belongs to the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is time we began to realize that the people's money should be spent where it can render the greatest service to the greatest number of people in Canada.
I want to bring to the minister's attention- and I see he has gone and has left a substitute. If his assistant were to do what is really and truly in his mind I am sure he would see that that highway went the way that I am asking that it should go, namely, through the Yellowhead pass.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Ask him.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Put him on the spot.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen on my left say: "Put him on the spot." I say to them: I am not that kind of a boy. So far as you fellows are concerned you think that you can say certain things.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: You don't know the way to vote.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I don't have to vote the way that you tell me to, but you have to vote the way you are told.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: You have not got a mind of your own.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I want to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: If you have, you don't know how to use it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The provinces choose the route.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I am not talking about the way in which the provinces choose the route; I am not talking about that at all. We know that the province chooses the route. We know that the province has done what we think should not be done. I am talking in this house not for the provinces but what I feel is for the good of Canada. I want to say this. I have been a municipal man in this country for many years. I have come to realize that today Canada is on wheels, and we need good roads. If these gentlemen to my left want to know something-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: We do not want to know anything.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
No, you don't want to know anything. You never did anything but talk, in Ontario, as long as I have known Canada. And as far as this highway is concerned, I want to make it definitely clear that we have produced in western Canada, and these gentlemen on my left know that we have produced and done things in western Canada which have made them very well off, so that they could have good roads in eastern Canada. They have them in Ontario, and they have them there because they get the money from us in western Canada.
[Inaudible interruption.]
As one hon. member says, we never had money in western Canada. I want to tell hon. gentlemen that between 1920 and 1946 we produced in western Canada ten billion bushels of wheat. Who got the money for it? Yes, who got the money? The people of Ontario and Quebec; they got it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Boo! boo!

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
You can boo as much as you like, but I want to tell you that so far as you are concerned you have had your benefits from the people of western Canada. And I can tell you a little more, but I don't want to.
Supply-Resources and Development

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Tell me everything.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Maybe I would fill your ears too full. So far as we are concerned in western Canada, we want a highway for that part of our country. We will not have the money to provide a highway of the standard we should have. Therefore we have to come to the federal authorities for help. If that highway is to be in the southern part of the province it will cost a great deal of money; that money will be spent down there in the building of the highway, and the people in the northern part of the province will be taxed to keep the highway in condition. Only a limited amount of money can be taxed in western Canada for highway purposes.
In Saskatchewan alone we have more highway service than Manitoba and Alberta put together. We have to provide highway facilities to more people than use such facilities. I want to bring this to the attention of the minister, that it is going to be a very serious thing for the people of Saskatchewan. It does not matter which government is in power in that province, because only a certain amount of money can be spent on highway construction. I am asking the minister to see that something is done to provide a highway system in the northern part of the three western provinces.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: They will not pay any attention to you; you do not vote the way you think.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not for nothing that I rise to delay the passage of this item, and particularly at this stage of the session when I know all hon. members wish to finish the work. Indeed, I believe many of them have made reservations for their passage home.
However, I am so dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement, from the point of view of the dominion government and the federal treasury, that I feel we are justified in delaying the passage of the item until we have had some further discussion. Had the minister been here I should have liked to ask him three questions, and the first would be this: Are the terms of the agreement being lived up to by the provinces?
From evidence gathered to date it is my understanding that those terms are not being lived up to, and nothing is being done to see that they carry out their side of the agreement. That agreement calls for certain specifications and, secondly, that it shall follow the shortest feasible route. I am not particularly interested in Ontario, but I am
4234	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development told that the route as laid out in this province is 160 miles longer than it should be. Certainly that is not carrying out the terms of the agreement.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Keep to your own province.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Coming to those provinces in western Canada in which I am most interested, I find that the route laid down and accepted under the terms of the agreement is one hundred miles longer than would have been necessary had it taken a more northerly course, and a course which would have been more in keeping with the hopes and dreams of the Canadian people. Certainly that is true of the people in western Canada.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Mackenzie, according to reports which have been made the route is laid out along the southern part of the three prairie provinces in what might be called the dust bowl, within fifty miles of the international boundary. Just over that boundary line to the south there are several of what might be described as No. 1 highways.
We in Canada should build a trans-Canada highway worthy of the title. What could be more embarrassing than for us to proceed in a manner whereby we would accept, as I believe some governments are expecting the federal government to do, number two and number three grade highways as part of the trans-Canada system. We would end up with the federal treasury paying 75 per cent of the cost and still not have a highway worthy of the name.
To show that this dissatisfaction did not arise since we came to this session of parliament, or since the item appeared in the estimates, I should like to read a letter which appeared in one of the Winnipeg papers several months ago. It was in reply to an editorial that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press and indicates that our satisfaction with the agreement certainly is not all that might be desired. I shall tell you who wrote the letter after I have finished reading it. It reads:
Commendations are in order for the keen interest the Free Press is taking in the proposed trans-Canada highway. In your leading editorial of December 1, 1949, however, you have left at least some of your readers rather confused as to just where you do stand on the all-important issue of standard plus location.
Then he quotes the editorial:
"The new highway has been too much discussed in terms of parochial benefits and not enough in terms of nationhood."
The letter continues:
And, further on in your editorial you state: "As far as Manitoba is concerned one-third of the work has already been done." Where the confusion arises, Mr. Editor, is as to which road you are referring to."


I pause here to point out that the one-third of the highway through Manitoba referred to in the editorial is the portion from Winnipeg to Brandon. The letter continues:
Surely not the present No. 1 highway from Winnipeg to Brandon for if this at best third-rate highway is to be the standard of a trans-Canada or coast to coast highway, then God forbid that we should be so nationally indiscreet, so prejudiced, so short-sighted as to think that we can fool other Canadians and much less Americans, by designating a third-rate highway by a first-rate name.
If we are to keep our Canadians travelling east and west in Canada and attract Americans to do the same we will have to do better than that. As the writer sees it, the thing that is bedevilling the issue in Manitoba and likely in most other provinces is the painful amount of selfish parochialism. As you so well put it, Mr. Editor, we must, if the highway is to justify the expenditure, make it so good in standard and location as to be not only a practical alternative to the highways of the United States: it must be even more attractive, more appealing.
^ To continue with your editorial, what does the "shortest practical east-west route consistent with the needs of the provinces" mean? Does it mean a wandering road, meandering here and there to take in as many local communities and constituencies as possible? If the reports we get here are even half true that is exactly what some provincial governments would do.
For example, reports reaching Ottawa, in some cases from provincial government level, are to the effect that the route already chosen by them is through the extreme south or dust bowl of the prairie provinces, and will meander around to the extent of lengthening the distance over the three prairie provinces by more than a hundred miles-
And that is correct.
-in excess of what would be necessary if a more northerly route was taken-
That is what the hon. member for Mackenzie suggested.
-and one eminently more desirable, and passing as it would through our wooded areas, closer to our many beautiful lakes surrounded with summer resorts, and above all closer to our magnificent western parks second to none.
I might point out that the number of people who visited Riding Mountain national park in Manitoba last year almost exceeded the number who visited Banff, and the way it is progressing perhaps in another year or two it will be Canada's No. 1 park. Yet we are going to skip it, not go near it. Apparently we do not want the public to see it. The letter continues:
Yes, Mr. Editor, politics and shortsighted parochial benefits may, if left unchecked, bedevil and destroy the hopes and dreams of millions of Canadians in the pleasure and economic benefits to be derived from a real trans-Canada highway.
There is a world of truth in that statement. As the highway is now laid out through western Canada there are no trees, lakes or parks. Neither is there any fishing or boating. There is nothing to attract anyone. To go back a few years to the period

of drought in Saskatchewan-and there are some from Saskatchewan who will remember this better than I do-I recall driving through that province on one occasion when I had to drive most of the way from the Manitoba boundary to Regina with my car in low gear in order to plow through the sand that was blowing across the country. Is that the show we want to put on for our United States friends and others when they visit our part of the country? I do not think so.
If we take the more northerly route we can save 100 miles in the distance across western Canada and we would tap some of the finest lakes in the country. Although I represent the district in which Dauphin is located, I am not particularly interested whether the road goes that way, but if it does then it will pass through timber country where there are many fine summer resorts and good fishing and boating. In the district of Grand View and the Duck mountain area there are eight or ten beautiful lakes. The mountain rises 2,700 feet above sea level. It is a wooded area with fine spruce, jackpine and other types of trees. Last year the provincial government constructed a good highway to Duck mountain. There are many beautifully treed lakes around the mountain. There are lakes like lake Laurier, named after Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Blue lake, as blue as the ocean, Child's lake, Wellman lake, and Jack-fish lake. They are all good fishing and boating lakes with excellent summer resorts, but we are going to skip all this.
The more northerly route would then proceed west to the region of Madge lake in the constituency of the hon. member for Mackenzie where there are beautiful summer resorts and lovely wooded country. Then it would continue westward to Saskatoon and Edmonton, and last but not least, the Alaska highway and the Yellowhead pass. There is everything to attract the public to travel over a route in the more northerly part of our western provinces, while there is nothing at all in the south. There must be an answer, and that is what I want to ask the minister. I should like to know why the terms of the agreement are being ignored, why the shortest practical route is not being followed, and why we are accepting third-rate highways, referred to in the letter which I read as a part of the trans-Canada highway. It would appear to me that we will end up with no trans-Canada highway at all. It is so ridiculous to think that out of the conglomeration of bits and scraps of roads across Canada we are going to build a trans-Canada highway and the dominion treasury is going to pay for it.
We have undertaken to pay 50 per cent of the cost of roads already constructed, and 55946-268
Supply-Resources and Development many of them are already worn out. I know they are in the province of Manitoba. They are only third-rate highways, and that is no reflection upon that province because they are just as good there as they are in most other provinces, and probably better than some. What we will have will be a highway that will not be worthy of the name "trans-Canada", just as the letter pointed out. Could anything be more embarrassing to the travelling public, to Mr. and Mrs. America who come to Canada to travel over our new highway, only to find that instead of the highway they had dreamed of and heard of up here in Canada, they must travel on only a third rate road? I can imagine Mr. and Mrs. America coming to Manitoba, perhaps from the northwest states, intending to go west over our trans-Canada highway, and coming to the city of Winnipeg. As the highway is laid out now it could not follow a more tortuous route, taking people right through the heart of the city. What could be more ridiculous? They would be lost before they got out of Winnipeg. Then when they had travelled another forty miles west Mr. America would think surely they must be on the wrong highway. Mrs. America would say, "No, the sign says trans-Canada highway." So they drive on and at the next town inquire where they missed the trans-Canada highway, only to be told that they are still on it.
Then they drive on through the sandhills, over a second or third class highway to Brandon. When they get there they find that the road takes a sharp turn down a steep hill crossing a long, narrow bridge, with room for only two cars, over the C.P.R. tracks. Again they will be lost before they get out of Brandon. When they do. get out of that city, what do they find? Talk about a dog's hind leg; no dog had a leg as crooked as the route from Brandon to the Saskatchewan boundary. Then when they get to Saskatchewan it is still worse; and that is to be the trans-Canada highway.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if we are going to spend $300 million on a highway we should start right. There may be an answer; there may be some reason for the rush to build the trans-Canada highway out of these bits of roads we now have. If there is we should be told the answer; but I do say this question should have been fully discussed on the floor of parliament before any agreement was entered into or a dollar was pledged. I do not want to delay the committee, though many other things could be said in opposition to the proposed route. The trans-Canada highway should be better

Supply-Resources and Development than the other highways; it should be something that would be a credit to Canada, that would make those travelling over it want to come back again and again to see our country. For goodness sake let us put it through that part of the country which has some attraction for tourists, not through the dust bowl of western Canada.
I am told the situation in Ontario is just as bad as anywhere else, and perhaps a little worse. I am told that parochialism has so bedevilled the plan in Ontario that they are taking the highway away down around by Peterborough. The hon. member for Peterborough West must be a good1 pleader to have the highway extended 160 miles further than it should be.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: That is a new highway, and they have to come to Peterborough, which is the best part of Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
That is just an example of what the editorial meant when it referred to provincialism and parochialism. Why, the way the highway wanders around western Canada, nearly every cabinet minister has had it come through his constituency; and we are asked to vote $300 million to build a road like that, which some day will bring us terrific embarrassment.
I do not know whether these words will do any good. I very seldom speak in the house because I have discovered that talking does not do much good. About eighty-five per cent of the speeches made this session were not listened to by anyone, and that is pretty well true of every session. I do my work outside, where I hope it is more effective. I made every appeal possible to the minister to try to prevent this thing happening, but the agreements were signed. I noticed that someone down in Nova Scotia was hesitating about signing it. Well, if that man belongs to the provincial government there is something wrong with his head if he hesitates to sign this agreement, because if ever anything was loaded in favour of the provinces, this is.
I have no objection in the world to the federal government giving the provinces some money for the construction of roads. That is all right, but let us not call those roads a trans-Canada highway. If we do we will only fool ourselves and others. If we want to give the provinces money to help them build roads, all right; but when we set out to build a trans-Canada highway let us build one worthy of this country. We are a great country, a big country, a wealthy country. We prate about our standards, our prestige in international affairs, and so on. Let us build a highway that will be a credit

to Canada, that both Canadians and Americans will talk about and be proud of. Let us not build a road that will be forever an embarrassment to all of us.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: The hon. member who has just taken his seat wondered why the highway should go through Peterborough. I believe No. 7 highway was selected because it is practically new; it has been paved and is almost as smooth as the rug on the floor of this chamber. It goes through the centre of the greatest tourist area in Canada, through Peterborough, Victoria and Lindsay and up through the Muskoka lakes. By going through Peterborough the people of Toronto and other highly populated sections have a chance to reach that highway without having to travel a great many more miles.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: In view of the representations that have been made, does the parliamentary assistant think the trans-Canada route should go through Edmonton?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I am going to help the parliamentary assistant answer that question; we have been friends for a long time, and I am sure he will be grateful. It does seem to me that we are wasting a great deal of time. This matter has been settled for so long that perhaps many of us have forgotten. To hear some people speak you would think they had never heard of Banff or Lake Louise, but in spite of their short memories those two most popular resorts in Canada are still doing business. I was interested in hearing the last speaker tell us about the attractions of his constituency, and I am quite prepared to admit them; I am sure it is the garden of the world. He forgot two of the main attractions on the route he suggested, however; one is gophers, and the other is mosquitoes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: It is too late now to change the decision to permit the province to decide the route, but the natural and proper route for the trans-Canada highway east and west is through Edmonton to the city of Prince Rupert. That would join the great Cariboo highway on the one hand, and the Alaska highway to the north. Tonight the Pacific ocean is the centre of world attention, and Prince Rupert, as my hon. friend from Skeena would say, is two or three days closer to the ports of Asia than any other port on the American continent. It is a strategic city, a city of great promise in the future from an industrial angle. The proper place for the trans-Canada highway is to bisect Canada at depth, and pass through the city of Edmonton through the priceless tourist area of Jasper to Prince George and to the seaport of Prince Rupert.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I should like to say a few words, but I am not going to become involved in the controversy over the route. The specifications laid down at the dominion-provincial * conference last December are being rigidly adhered to by the provinces. I would remind hon. members that the agreement specifies that the route shall not only be the shortest, but the shortest practical route.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I would be glad if the newest province's share of the trans-Canada highway could be carried by somebody other than the newest province. One day this week the minister announced that the specifications for the Newfoundland part of it were going to be exactly the same as the specifications for all other provinces. When the provincial minister of public works came here in April to sign the contract, he said he could not sign it because he felt the specifications could not be met owing to the cost. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant what has happened to enable those specifications to be adhered to, and who is meeting the cost, if any?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand that in the case of Newfoundland, certain modifications of the specifications are now being considered under the agreement. It will still be a serviceable highway, but not of the standard required in more densely populated centres.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: You do not mean to tell me that the minister's statement was not correct?

Item agreed to.
Canadian Government Travel Bureau-
399. To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada, $1,514,421.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: There is a large item in this vote for advertising and publicity, amounting to nearly a million dollars. Will the parliamentary assistant tell us where this advertising is being conducted?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Before there is an answer, may I say something about Mr. Leo Dolan, who is in charge of the travel bureau. He has done an excellent job of advertising Canada in the United States. Due to his efforts-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I asked the parliamentary assistant to answer this question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not alone in the house, and while the parliamentary assistant weighs the argument he presented, I do not see why another member of parliament has not the right to speak. The hon. member who has put the question has no 55916-268 \
Supply-Resources and Development mortgage on the time of the house. He has an opportunity, in common with other members, to ask his question, and the parliamentary assistant has a right to answer whenever he feels he has to do so. In the meantime another member of parliament has unquestionably the right to say what e has to say about a matter of this kind involving an expenditure of a million and a half dollars.
I recall the time when another party was in power, and we had the travel bureau. A large amount was spent under Mr. Manion, who was the leader of the Conservative party. He appreciated the work that was done by the travel bureau, and believed that Canada should be advertised. How many people in he United States are interested in Canada, but do not know much about it? It is my duty as a member of parliament to congratulate Mr. Dolan on having publicized Canada, as he has so successfully in so many of the large cities in the United States. He has made the tourist industry an important business in Canada. Very often I have complained about some civil servants, and I am pleased at this time to be able to say I am satisfied with one. I do so with the utmost pleasure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development
maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in answer to the member for Victoria (Ont.), the money is all spent in the United States.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have sat here all evening without making any comment on these items, and I intend to make a few comments on this item regardless of the "Oh's". First of all I am pleased to see there is an increase in this item of $216,000 because I think that this department is one which is well worth any extra expenditure. Before proceeding with the brief remarks I wish to make on this item, I want to say that I think Mr. Dolan and his staff are doing an excellent job. I have found evidence of that from people I know in the United States, and from people across Canada. One thing I liked from what I have seen of the staff of the Canadian travel bureau is that they actually do attempt to promote tourist travel in Canada. I believe there is excellent esprit de corps amongst the staff of the travel bureau.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to make my annual speech on this subject, and to urge again that as much advertising as possible be undertaken of the smaller resources in Canada, whether they be in central Canada, western Canada or any other part. We can leave the advertising of the larger resorts, such as Lake Louise, Jasper, the Seigniory club and the Chateau Frontenac to the railroads. I noticed an excellent article in the

Supply-Resources and Development Christian Science Monitor dealing with tourist opportunities in Canada. It dealt entirely with the larger resorts in Canada. Mr. Chairman, there is a small percentage of the Canadian people of modest means, or people from the United States of modest means, who are able to visit the larger resorts. The average Canadian of modest means wants to attend a place at modest cost, where he can have his meals without having to put on his best bib and tucker. I do urge that everything be done to advertise the resorts all across Canada that are operated by the smaller people for the smaller people of modest means. That would be my only criticism of the literature published by the Canadian travel bureau. There happen to be in my constituency numbers of very excellent small resorts which some of the members of the House of Commons visit periodically. We have fishing, hunting, swimming, boating, mountain climbing, hot springs and skiing in the riding of Kootenay West. On the Kootenay lake we have the Kootenay cottages, Kootenay bay resorts, the beautiful Balfour beaches and resorts, the areas around Nelson, the north shore, and the beautiful fishing camps and resorts around the city of Kaslo. In the Arrow Lake district we have Halcyon hot springs for those who want medical treatment and Saint Leon hot springs for those who want to sun bathe, fish, hunt or swim. We have the lovely district around Nakusp and we have the district of Deer Park and the Lardeau where any member of this committee can go and be certain of getting a grizzly bear in the season at any time. In addition to that we have the remarkable community enterprise in the Rossland ski lift on Red mountain.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: Krestova.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
An hon. member opposite mentions Krestova, but that would be a tourist resort from an entirely different angle from the one I am mentioning now.
I do urge that these smaller resorts throughout Canada be advertised to the fullest extent because they are the type of resorts that the bulk of the American people of modest means and the bulk of Canadian people of modest means want and are able to patronize; and they are operated by people of small and modest means. In the district of southeastern British Columbia one finds 40,000 square miles of mountain scenery, and everything the tourist delights to enjoy. I do urge in conclusion that the full facilities of this bureau be used to advertise the beautiful but smaller and in many cases almost unknown resorts in Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I want to ask the minister one question. I should like him to ask his highly efficient travel director, the next time he is in Montreal, if he will tell the Canadian Pacific Railway that there is $300 million invested every year or spent every year in skiing. Along the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway is the finest skiing in the world and practically nothing is being done about it. I wish that the government would try to nudge the railway to do something about it because we have the greatest potential tourist asset along that main line of any anywhere, not only in North America but anywhere in the world.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I want to ttiank the minister for answering my question. I am glad they are doing their advertising in the large cities of the United States, because I feel that the American tourist industry is one that can be developed. We have quite a number of American tourists coming up into our section of the country each and every year; and more are coming year by year. These American tourists, our cousins, make arrangements for anywhere from $200 to $3,500 per family in American exchange when they are coming over here. They make that arrangement before they come here, so that I know they are spending a great deal of money. We know from the banks the amount of American money that perhaps is collected from time to time in our local banks. It is a great asset to us to have the American tourists come in here. It is new money. It is therefore fine for everybody within our area. I am saying thanks to the minister, and I am glad they are spending as much money as possible in promoting the tourist industry and advertising in the United States.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
I find myself in sympathy both with the C.C.F. gentleman and with the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.). On opening the New York Times the other day I read a wonderful article dealing with the Alaska highway. Nobody had paid for the article; I mean, it was not an advertisement; it was a descriptive article dealing with the Alpine attractions or the tourist attractions of that area. I found out later that it had been placed there by this agency which is under this department. The Chicago Tribune also from time to time, in its Sunday edition, carries extensive articles dealing with northern British Columbia and the Yukon, and the attractions there. It costs us nothing but still these articles are written and the photographs are supplied by Mr. Leo Dolan and his department here in Ottawa.
I think that there are two sources of foreign exchange coming into Canada this summer. One is the sale of our gold and the

other is the receipt of American dollars from the tourist traffic. In the little rock garden represented by the hon. member for Kootenay West there are many attractions, but you can go a thousand miles from there and the attractions increase as you go north. This department is presenting those attractions favourably to the tourists.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext: I understand that the gentleman you know as "Mr. Travel" is going to Newfoundland in the next two months to assist in the promotion of the tourist industry. I want him to know that, with his past record, we are looking ahead with great interest to the work he is going to do. As far as Newfoundland is concerned, we wish him all sorts of luck. I am speaking of Mr. Dolan.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR LOCATION OF MAIN LINE ENTIRELY WITHIN CANADA
speechtext:
I have been interested in the development of the tourist trade ever since the department at Ottawa was established at the instance, I may say, of Senator W. H. Dennis of Halifax. I agree with what has been said with respect to the director, Mr. Dolan, the one who took over this work at the very beginning. It is true that he has been under many ministers in the intervening years. I suppose if he got a little bit of wisdom from each of those ministers, it would be some explanation of the development.
Since the department was established we have gone through some unfortunate years of depression and war. The construction of highways has greatly interfered with tourist traffic. I hope and expect to see greater development in the years directly ahead. If there is one criticism or wish that I might express, it is that more attention should be given to the people in central Canada, to whom we in the maritimes have contributed so much, to encourage them to visit the maritime provinces. There are a number of them who do come down to the maritimes, but a great many go to other places, especially to Maine in the United States, and who should properly come to the maritime provinces and in particular to Nova Scotia which has attractions for tourists unequalled anywhere in any country.
Item agreed to.
269. Departmental administration, $1,353,625.

We have been a long time getting to this department, but we are there. We were on this item at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, when you and I had a little difference of opinion about the time, whether it was 5-59 or 6-01. Eventually it was called six o'clock.
Supply-Post Office
The item before us is one of the principal items in the Post Office estimates. I wish to direct a few remarks to the Postmaster General. As I said at the beginning, I endorse the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Peel with regard to the minister's return to the house, and also his remarks with regard to the setting up of a committee at another session.
The Postmaster General gave a very good account of the work of his department and of the increase in sales in his department amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. We always look upon the Post Office Department as a department that has the opportunity of making large profits. I now ask the minister what was the net profit in the Post Office Department in the last fiscal year. In other years it has been as high as $13 million. With the volume of business that the department has done the net revenue I suppose will be larger than ever. I do not know whether he gave the figure when he was speaking this afternoon.
There is nothing in business that can be produced cheaper than a four-cent postage stamp. It produces the greatest profit of anything that can possibly be produced. Its sales are the largest in the entire department. In this connection I notice one item here that is a Uttle bit discouraging. I refer to the mail service of Canada. An amount of $11,859,213 was paid last year for the mail services by ordinary land conveyance, including rural mail delivery. There is no breakdown for the year 1951 to show what it will be, but in this vote which includes air mail delivery as well as the rural courier delivery, there is a decrease of almost a million dollars, to be exact $948,264. Whether or not this decrease comes entirely out of the earnings of the rural mail couriers is something that I should like to know from the Postmaster General.
The problem of mail couriers has been with us for years. On many occasions in the house and in committee it has been discussed. When we were discussing the vote in 1946 the then Postmaster General promised to set up a committee to study the problem of the rural mail couriers. However, he did not last too long in office, and went out with the promise unfulfilled. If you compare vote 269 with 270, 269 dealing with mail couriers and 270 dealing with the employees of the central offices, you will find quite a difference. During last year there was an increase in salaries amounting to something over $4,450,000, but, as I said, at the same time the rural mail couriers took a decrease of almost a million dollars. I am not objecting to the salaries paid to these officials, but I do object to the

Supply-Post Office
decrease that was handed out to the rural mail couriers, because they are the people who distribute the mail and finally get it out to the people in the different parts of the country.
I might say that there is no class of servant in this country serving the public or His Majesty that can compare to the mail couriers. They have a hard job, and they do it well. I want to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to what happened in Prince Edward Island during last year, and to the mail couriers in my constituency, and I can speak for most of them. They have always been excellent couriers. Some of them have been in the service from 18 to 45 years, and are still key men. They have never had a complaint registered against them either by the public or by the department. I want to mention one of these men who had a mail route of about 28 to 30 miles. During the Christmas season last year we had very bad road conditions in Prince Edward Island. This courier was so anxious to serve the public, especially during the holiday season, when it was impossible for him to take a car over the dirt roads and he found that he could not make it with a horse and rig, that he went and hired a jeep. He also hired a driver for that jeep, and for six days he went with the driver of the jeep and delivered the mail, and did it on time. It cost that mail courier $9 a day for six days, which is quite a sum, besides his own costs. That is the type of men we have down there. I saw another man on the road at one time during that season when it was muddy. He took a car for seven miles on the highway. At the end of the seven miles he had to have a horse and wagon. He drove five miles more with them, and when he got to the end of those five miles there was a crossroad where there was from three to five feet of snow and he had to have a horse and sleigh to cover that distance. Then he had to double back over that same road. I just mention this because the contract of one of these men came up. I say the department should give careful consideration to a faithful man and give him a contract at a reasonable rate, one which would permit him to live and not necessitate his going into debt or to suffer undue hardship. However, the department said that it was not agreeable, and that it felt this work could be done for less money. It was further pointed out that tenders must be called for.
Where a man has given good service for a good many years, and continues to give it, where a man is prepared to serve the people properly, the Postmaster General and the department should be able to figure out what his services are worth so that he can be paid
[Mr. McLure.l
accordingly. It is all- very well to say that the average price per mile in Prince Edward Island is $53.
That is the average.

Yes, the average. That may be so, but at the same time that is where the discrimination comes in. For instance, I know of mail routes in Prince Edward Island where they get only $35 a mile, and I know of others where they get as high as $87 a mile.
I could mention one route in particular where the contract calls for $2,400. That is not too much money-not a nickel too much for the 28 or 29 miles that must be travelled. However, I know of another man who travels 27 miles over a harder route and who receives only $1,625, or about two-thirds of the former amount. That is where the discrimination comes in under the present tendering system. The sooner this department can establish some principle whereby it could figure out what would be fair and honest for all these drivers, the better it will be for the service. So much for the mail couriers.
Then, I have another matter to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General, namely one having to do with an official who has been in the service for a long time as stamp vendor. He is now serving his forty-ninth year in the service, is still going strong and giving good service. He has not been pensioned off, and I am told that he has no opportunity of receiving any pension. This man is working under contract and cannot be dismissed unless it is shown that he is not giving proper service.
However, after serving for forty-nine years, without complaint either from the public or from the department, it is time something was done for him. Let us look at his contract. It states that he shall go to work at eight o'clock in the morning and must keep his office open until eight o'clock in the evening every day of the week except Sunday. Every year he is allowed two or three statutory holidays.
Let me contrast this with the average clerk in the postal department. The man to whom I am referring works a day and a half for every day the ordinary clerk works. Therefore, contrasting this man with a clerk, it is clear that while a clerk was working forty-nine years this man would have worked seventy-three.
His contract stipulates that he shall receive as payment two per cent on all sales. He applied for an increase in that percentage when the cost of living drove expenses higher and higher, but was unsuccessful in

his application, and was reminded of the terms of the contract under which he had been operating. What happened? To get rid of this man who had been giving good service, meters were installed. I have no objection at all to stamp meters. According to his contract however he should have received two per cent on all meter sales. Despite the fact that his revenue has been cut in half, the Post Office Department does not allow him that two per cent on meter sales.
I say it is a mean thing when we find a big department such as this one trying to get rid of an employee by taking away his sales through the installation of a meter system. The time has come when this man should be given some kind of pension. I hope my suggestion will not be brushed off, because the plight of this man stands as a blot against the department. He has been working at a low wage, but the department is now proceeding to make something extra by taking sales away from him through the installation of stamp meters.
Last year we discussed the promise to reduce the postage rate from four cents to three cents. I would rather see it retained at four cents until such time as the mail couriers are properly paid for the work they do. I hope it will not be reduced until those people have received something for the fine service they have rendered.
In the post office at Charlottetown there are excellent officials, but the objection I have always taken is that while Prince Edward Island is a province, we have been tacked on to New Brunswick in this particular. We should have the very same rights as any other province-and we are going to get them some day. While this government discriminates against Prince Edward Island, there will be a change of government some day and we will get rid of the discrimination. There is no justice in our being tacked on to any other province. We are a province in ourselves, and according to the terms of our contract of 1873 we are entitled to whatever any other province can have, even though it be on a smaller scale. I would ask the Postmaster General to answer this point.
I would ask the Postmaster General to take up with the Minister of Public Works the matter of a new post office building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where?

The one there now is fair, but for the last six or seven years they have been drawing plans for a new one. When the final plans are prepared it will be up to the Postmaster General to see that the
Supply-Post Office
post office at Charlottetown is properly located in the new building that has been promised for such a long time. In closing,
I hope the Postmaster General will meet our request to set up a committee at the next session of the house for the purpose of studying the problems of the rural mail couriers, and laying down a policy by which they may have some sense of security and appropriate pay for their services.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On April 6 of this year there appeared in the Hartland Observer of Hart-land, New Brunswick, a news item to the effect that certain changes had been effected with regard to the postal service in that part of Carleton county. Apparently this item of news was rather offensive to one D. R. Bishop, who lives in Woodstock, New Brunswick, which is located in Carleton county. I find that a few days later he published a paid advertisement in the Hartland Observer taking exception to the news item that had appeared some days earlier. I should like to call the attention of the Postmaster General to two or three sentences in this paid advertisement over the name of D. R. Bishop. They are:
I have documents in my file on this matter-
The matter has to do with certain changes in postal delivery.
-to show that I and no one else made all arrangements concerning this matter. Every detail concerning the cancellation of the original plan of the department, the setting up of a new route, additions to the new one, and as to what post offices would be closed, was arranged by me with the department. That can be clearly proven by records not only in my office but by records and road maps sent by me to Post Office Department at Ottawa.
The advertisement continues, but I need not bother reading it all. As I have already indicated, it is over the name of D. R. Bishop, and apparently is an advertisement which he paid for. I was a bit shocked at this barefaced claim to what amounts to the control of patronage in that area, and I felt I would like to get more information about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is that in your capacity as parliamentary assistant to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is in my capacity as one who asked' a number of questions earlier in the session concerning patronage, the answers to which may be found on Hansard. As a matter of fact, on page 352 of Hansard for this session the Prime Minister told me that there were no official records indicating patronage. At page 842 of Hansard for this session he said to me:
The only knowledge I have of anything of that kind is that one of the defeated candidates in a by-election asked ipe who was going to handle

Supply-Post Office
patronage. I told him that to my knowledge there was no patronage, that there were persons who made certain recommendations to which more or less importance was attached, but that was all there was to it.
The Prime Minister went on to complain about my putting questions of that nature on the order paper. The assurance of the Prime Minister that there was no such thing as patronage really did not convince me, and from time to time during the session I have had instances of it drawn to my attention.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: By whom?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is one to which I have just referred.
Is that a reliable newspaper?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
At least the advertisement was paid for by Mr. D. R. Bishop who, I have learned, by checking the parliamentary guide and other documents, was the Liberal candidate in the constituency of Victoria-Carleton in the election held a year ago today. It is quite fitting that we should deal with this matter today. I felt that this claim on the part of Mr. D. R. Bishop that he was telling the post office what to do in Carleton county was one that needed to be investigated. I put a rather all-inclusive motion on the order paper asking for the return of papers concerning this matter, feeling that I would either get the papers and see that Mr. Bishop was right, that he is in charge of patronage down there, and thus patronage would be revealed, or that there would be nothing on the record and he would be shown to be wrong.
It turns out that Mr. Bishop is substantially correct. As a matter of fact, sessional paper No. 85K, tabled on Wednesday, June 21, 1950, in answer to the motion I put on the order paper, reveals even more information than I asked for. By going through this document of some ninety-four pages, I discovered that not only does Mr. D. R. Bishop, the defeated Liberal candidate in that area, have a good deal of influence with the Post Office Department, but so does the senator from that region, to whom communications are addressed from time to time.
I rise deliberately to complain about the affairs of the Post Office Department being handled in this way. It seems to me that it ought to be on a civil service basis, or on a business basis, but not on a patronage basis.
Let me draw your attention to a couple of letters in the file which, as I say, my motion produced even though I did not know they were there. At page 78 of the file I find a letter addressed to the Hon. F. W. Pirie, the Senate, Ottawa, Ontario, over the

signature of one of the officials in the operations branch of the Post Office Department. In the letter Senator Pirie is informed that there is a certain vacancy at Mineral, New Brunswick, in the electoral district of Victoria-Carleton. It does not say it is in Carleton county; it is in the constituency of Victoria-Carleton. Then there is this sentence:
Would you be good enough, therefore, to submit for the consideration of the Postmaster General, on the official form attached, your recommendation of a suitable person who will be willing to accept this position.
What is the date of the letter?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Was his advice good or bad?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just a minute-
Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I turn to page 72 and I find a letter from the director of operations of the Post Office Department. The department is ready to make the appointment to the post office at Mineral, New Brunswick, but there is this letter of July 21, 1947, to the Hon. F. W. Pirie, Grand Falls, New Brunswick. It states that the department is ready to confirm the appointment of Mr. So and So, but then there is this paragraph:
Before issuing instructions the department would like to know whether Mr. Kinney's appointment meets with your approval. An official form is attached for your convenience.
I remind hon. members that the Prime Minister assured me there was no such thing as patronage, no one handled it, and one of the reasons that one of my questions about patronage could not be answered was that there was nothing on the record. I now have some of the material respecting patronage that is on the record by the medium of asking this question about what is going on in the electoral district of Victoria-Carleton. In this paid advertisement Mr. D. R. Bishop states that he has documents, letters and maps to show that he is responsible for the arrangements that have been made at some of these places such as Holmesville, Mineral, Moose Mountain and so on, and sure enough in the sessional paper for which I asked here are the maps that Mr. Bishop drew and submitted, which apparently have become the basis for the routes that have been established down there. In this file are at least three maps submitted by this same Mr. Bishop.
What are the maps?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
They are maps of rural routes for that area. Then I look at page 34 of this interesting file and find a lengthy

letter under date of January 20, 1950, over the signature of Mr. G. Herring, director of communications, addressed to Mr. D. R. Bishop, Woodstock, New Brunswick, setting out the arrangements finally agreed upon for the postal service in this area. It reads exactly like a letter from an official at head office to an official out in the field; you would not think it was just to a defeated Liberal candidate, but there it is. It is lengthy, so I will not read it, but I will read the reply, which is businesslike and direct. It is addressed to Mr. Herring and reads:
Re Upper Kent R.R. No. 1
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 20. The arrangements mentioned in your letter seem to cover this matter excellently. Therefore I am very satisfied with them.
Very truly yours,
D. R. Bishop
There is no such thing as patronage, says the Prime Minister, and of course no one controls it; but Mr. Bishop certainly thinks he does. In a paid advertisement he claims he does, and the documents he says are on file certainly seem to be there. Then I come back to page 30, where I find that on February 6, 1950, Mr. Herring addressed a communication to Daniel R. Bishop, Woodstock, New Brunswick, as follows:
Re Bath rural route No. 3
I am enclosing herewith a copy of the notice inviting tenders for the above mentioned mail service together with form 95-A for your information.
Yours truly,
G. Herring,
Director of Communications
The next several pages consist of applications that were sent in response to the invitation to tender. Then another letter goes to Mr. Bishop from Mr. Herring on March 20, 1950, informing him that the department intends to award the contract for this service to Mr. Saunders Giberson, the lowest tenderer, at the rate of $1,200 per annum.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Anything wrong with that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No, but listen to the next letter, dated March 24, 1950:
Dear Mr. Herring,
I have received your letter of March 20, and have had several protests from very responsible people to the effect that the lowest tenderer in this case is and always has been a most irresponsible person.
It, therefore, would seem that an investigator should be sent up there before this contract is awarded to him.
Yours very truly,
D. R. Bishop
I suppose you would call that patronage in reverse. The next letter is dated March 30, and is from Mr. Herring back to Mr. Bishop,
Supply-Post Office
and I think hon. members should get this. It is a most interesting document, and if you did not know who Mr. D. R. Bishop was you would think this was an exchange of correspondence between an official at head office and a responsible official out in the field. But that man out in the field is just a fellow who was a Liberal candidate in the last election. In reply to Mr. Bishop's letter saying that Mr. Giberson is and has always been a most irresponsible person, which is a pretty sweeping statement to make about anybody, Mr. Herring wrote as follows:
Dear Mr. Bishop:
I have your letter of the 24th March with regard to the conveyance of mails over Bath rural route No. 3 and I note your remarks concerning the lowest tenderer.
In reply I may say that this matter will be looked into at once.
Yours very truly,
G. Herring,
Director of Communications
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Bishop did not take too long to reply. The previous letter was dated March 30, and this one back to Mr. Herring is dated April 3:
I have your letter of March 30 in answer to mine of the 24th. The matter is further complicated by the fact that the present tenderer has requested to be relieved of this contract forthwith.
The general opinion is as I stated in my former letter, but since no one will make any specific charge, I do not feel their complaints should be listened to, and would advise that this man begin his contract as quickly as possible.
Yours very truly,
D. R. Bishop
First of all the man writes a most damning letter saying this fellow is and always has been most irresponsible and should not get the job. Then a few weeks later he writes and reverses his decision, and says that Mr. Giberson should be appointed. On April 6 Mr. Herring replied to Mr. Bishop as follows:
With reference to your letter of the 3rd instant concerning contract arrangements for the conveyance of mails over Bath rural route No. 3, I wish to inform you that instructions have been issued awarding the contract to Mr. Saunders Giberson at $1,200 per annum, subject, of course, to his being in a position to perform service satisfactorily.
Yours very truly,
G. Herring,
Director of Communications
Who is this D. R. Bishop? First of all the department writes telling him that invitations to tender have been sent out. Later on they tell him that so-and-so is going to be awarded the contract. He says no, that fellow is no good; don't give it to him. The department says they will hold up the contract. Then Mr. Bishop thinks it over again and says Mr. So-and-So should get the job, and he gets it.

Supply-Post Office
I could go on, because this is a most interesting file, but I think the point has been established that this hardly conforms to the assurance the Prime Minister sought to give me that there was no such thing as patronage anywhere in the government service, that there was no such thing as defeated Liberal candidates having certain powers in connection with these matters. The hon. member for Red Deer says he knows now why a parliamentary committee will never be appointed to look into post office matters. Not many days ago I had something to say about this same Mr. D. R. Bishop in connection with another department. That stirred up a bit of interesting newspaper comment down in that part of the country, and I find that a letter has been brought to light which this Mr. Bishop circulated before the last election, and even before the Liberal nomination in that constituency. In that letter, which apparently was sent to a number of people and which is reprinted in The Observer of Hartland, New Brunswick, of June 22, 1950. Mr. Bishop said:
You will therefore understand what may seem to be my inaction, but after Saturday I will be around in support of whoever the convention chooses. As you know, I do not particularly want this nomination, but with a new four-lane highwav to be constructed under federal supervision from Grand Falls to Eel River, it means a lot of money will be spent here, and that somebody must be in charge of it.
As I say, hon. members must not forget the positive assurance I was given by the Prime Minister on March 1, 1950, at page 352 of Hansard and on March 16, 1950, at page 842, that there is no such thing as patronage in the government service and no such thing as defeated Liberal candidates having any say in connection with these matters.
Mr. Chairman, we hear about this sort of thing too often. It just so happens that in this instance one has the evidence. There is more if I want to take the time to read it. If hon. members desire to know about it I advise them to look at sessional paper No. 89C of March 18, 1948; 89E of April 27, 1948 and 87E of April 25, 1949. They will find that all those sessional papers, brought down on motions of other members of the house, produce documents showing the influence that Liberal members of parliament and defeated Liberal candidates seek to bring to bear upon the Post Office Department with respect to its affairs. We know that when there are vacancies in the postal service, advice is sent to the Liberal members. We hear of that from time to time. We do not get it. We do not want it.
Oh, oh.
I have taken a note of that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish the extent of that Liberal laughter could be properly recorded in Hansard. The fact of the matter is that Liberals are so immersed in this business of patronage and controlling things their way that they cannot understand anyone not wanting to be a party to it in any way, shape or form. I am protesting against patronage in so far as there is full evidence of it in sessional paper 85K; I am protesting against it in so far as we hear of its taking place in various places. I do insist there is need for getting rid of this kind of thing in the Post Office Department. I strongly support the suggestions that have been made during the course of this debate today that there should be a committee to o into post office matters-not just into the question of the rural mail couriers, but into T e whole question of the post office as it is run

with particular reference to the part that senators, Liberal members of parliament and defeated Liberal candidates play in relation to post office matters.

I just want to say a word in answer to my hon. friend. He has read some excerpts from letters by Mr. Bishop an-1 Mr. Herring, acknowledged in a natural way, in a democratic way. Canadian citizens in New Brunswick did write to the department and they were answered by the department much better than I am myself as a member of parliament. I ask a question of my hon. friend, and I am speaking of the Bishop-Herring file. The most important thing in what he has said is not whether the suggestion came from Bishop or from anyone else: the question is whether the suggestion made by a New Brunswicker to the department is a good one or a bad one. My hon. friend did not discuss that point. The most important point in connection with the business is not who made the suggestion, but the suggestion itself. I challenge my hon. friend to say that the advice given to the Post Office Department by Bishop was not good.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Which advice? The advice to hire him or not to hire him?

Both. I challenge the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton to repeat what has been said by the member for Winnipeg North Centre. He will not dare touch it because it happened in his own constituency. It is better for the Post Office Department to listen to Bishop of New Brunswick about New Brunswick matters than to listen to the member for Winnipeg North Centre. The member for Winnipeg North Centre is one of my colleagues for whom I have great admiration. I admire his industry, and I

admire his good intentions; but he does not know anything about the post office business in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about patronage?

Patronage is a good thing. Those who pretend to the contrary and do not know about it may be excused. Those who pretend to the contrary and know about it are just hypocrites. It is essential that the Post Office Department or any other department should be informed by men in whom the government has confidence, and who will not betray the government in the advice they give to the department. Is it clear now?
If the department were to listen to the Tories about recommendations, the department would be led into error. If a Conservative government had been in power and the member for Victoria-Carleton had been a supporter of the Tory government, he would never have been able to give such good advice as Bishop did. I have great admiration for him, and I have more admiration for the way he used the member for Winnipeg North Centre as his dummy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege, I think the hon. member on reflection would rather not be recorded as making that statement. The member for Victoria-Carleton, knowing I am interested in this question of patronage, showed me the original advertisement to which I referred. Members of this house who know me do not need to be told a second time that, the minute I saw it I decided I was going to do something about it-on my own. I do not even know whether the member for Victoria-Carleton likes my taking this up, and I do not care whether he does or not. To me it was a most bare-faced claim to be in control of patronage, and I was concerned to find out all I could about it.
While I am on my feet may I say to the member for Temiscouata that when he tells me the government Post Office Department should get its advice from people in whom it has confidence, I agree. The department, however, should get its advice from the officials who the department knows are experts in the field. I am not suggesting they should get advice from the member for Victoria-Carleton, or from the member for Temiscouata.
I would not touch it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am suggesting that we pay considerable sums of money for civil servants in this department, so that the department can have experts to decide on these matters. As for the matter of a person in whom someone has confidence, surely the member does not
Supply-Post Office
suggest that a candidate who has been rejected by the constituency is a person to whom the government should look as the man in whom to place confidence. Far better for the department to get its advice from its own experts in the field.

I will tell my friend one thing. If he is offended by the word "dummy" I will substitute an argument on the word and I will tell him that I never contended that he was magnetized or hypnotized by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. All I meant to say was that the member for Victoria-Carleton had made him believe that it was an awful thing, but did not go so far as to admit it. He has admitted that the member for Victoria-Carleton had shown the paper to him, and the light was on the paper, and it induced him to do a lot of work to find that file in which there was nothing wrong. He was easily scandalized.
Oh, oh.
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member for Temiscouata has already said that he wants patronage. We know where he stands.
If we continued that argument for five minutes, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would admit that I am right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, no. Never.
So much so that the hon. mem-be for Victoria-Carleton will never dare to repeat what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Oh, oh.

Carried.
